Hey everyone, [@kamaljeet.dhiman|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U043969T4JE] and I had a quick chat about promoting the score sharing by users. Copying the thoughts I shared with him for visibility and further comments (cc [@lev.goffert|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U05G55B6Y5B]):

* Strictly from legal and privacy standpoints, it’s fine if Bolt wants to encourage users to share their driving scores externally (e.g., on social media or via messages). Technically, users can already do this by taking screenshots for example.
* Still we should ensure we only facilitate sharing of simplified data. The data in the prototype should be fine, i.e., score, number of drives and mileage without including detailed score or ride history.
* That said, there are important practical implications to be considered. We’re already seeing users complaints and access requests, social media discussions, and negative PR with media outlets asking questions about the driving score. I personally believe it’s only a matter of time until authorities start asking questions too. Promoting score sharing will likely intensify this trend and accelerate further scrutiny.
* I don’t want to focus only on the negatives, and I know we’re also receiving positive feedback. However, from where I’m sitting it’s hard to assess if the benefits of score sharing outweigh the potential risks brought by the additional exposure.
* My personal feeling is that it would be prudent to gather more insights before actively promoting the driving score beyond the Bolt App, and not just in terms of sharing the score. I anticipate that the rollout in Berlin will serve as an important test with good learning opportunities.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
The agreement is not aligned with our operating model. It makes Bolt a *data processor with far-reaching and significantly challenging requirements applicable to Bolt.* Normally, under GDPR/RODO Bolt acts as a controller, where such requirements are not applicable.

 *What this means in practice* - *accepting the draft status creates significant risks:*

# *Operational impossibility* – examples: needing customer approval for suppliers that Bolt engages, needing customer consent to transfer data outside the EU.
# *Full liability is indicated for non-compliance with data protection laws & customer's template.* Even if re-negotiate to limit the liability in the contract, GDPR keeps Bolt liable to the customer as a processor for its non-compliance, there is no way to lawfully limit this.
# *High Penalties* (50K ZLT) *indicated for non-compliance with data protection law & customer's template.*

I flagged most obvious high-risk issued in this [customer's document copy|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1LmjFO2S1lT7fUp5bpQPe3yoitjHjW_Gp/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=106326439712206242177&rtpof=true&sd=true] - translated to English, as I do not speak Polish.

*Good news:* The customer explains they need Bolt as processor because they themselves are a processor. However, this situation is not new – we have *successfully negotiated solutions* with such customers before.

* We also have a *ready template* where a customer acting as a processor (Partner) works with Bolt as controller (usually used with RideBooker API) - attached as file & explanatory note added to the draft.
* This can be reused for the case of this particular customer.

 *My recommendation:* share the above template with the customer, explain again we rely on this as a standard approach with customers who act as data processors, and propose a call to find a solution (I can join after vacation).

 Accepting their draft as-is = *high legal + operational risk* for Bolt.

I’ve conducted my initial analysis on the topic.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*TL;DR* 

Risk level: Low–Medium. Proceed if Rewards uses *only KPIs already active* in Thailand (e.g. finished rides, ratings, activity) and is framed as a voluntary benefit. Do not proceed if non-operational metrics (e.g. acceptance rate blocking) or punitive exclusions are introduced.
{panel}



+Contractual Fit+ 

* The Thai General Terms for Drivers clause 19.1 discloses three main parameters affecting allocation: Acceptance Rate, Driver Score, and ETA.
* As long as Rewards uses only these three metrics, the feature is covered by existing Terms.
* If any additional KPIs (like cancellations, utilization, or wait time) are introduced as part of Rewards tiering, then the General Terms for Drivers would need to be updated first to stay aligned.



+Risks and guardrails+

* Reclassification risk is low in Thailand (Class 1 market). Still, visibility of algorithmic perks in Rewards can create optics that drivers are being performance-managed.
* Participation in Rewards must remain voluntary, with no penalties or disadvantages for drivers who choose not to join.

* *Fine to proceed* if:
✔ Only the three existing metrics (Acceptance Rate, Driver Score, ETA) are used.
✔ Rewards is shown as a positive, optional benefit.
✔ Drivers outside Rewards still get normal matching (no exclusions, other than the existing 20-minute safeguard).
✔ Driver autonomy (accept/decline rights) remains intact.
* *Not fine to proceed* if:
✘ New/unfamiliar KPIs are added without updating Terms.
✘ Rewards is framed as mandatory to access rides.


*Please confirm which exact metrics/KPIs will be used for Rewards tiering.* If it’s only the three metrics in the terms (Acceptance Rate, Driver Score, ETA), we’re safe to proceed. If others are planned, I would need to adjust the terms first.

Hi [~accountid:63e3ef2dbf837c6893db58e3] - Sharing some initial thoughts from a privacy POV. The most important issues are highlighted in yellow.

*_* Please note we are still bottoming-out a few research points and will provide our final and complete advice in due course. The below is just intended to provide an overview of the key issues._*

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
*Marketing comms sent to passengers*
{panel}

* When a _passenger who does not have a Bolt account_ uses a kiosk, I understand that a profile is created for them on Bolt’s systems to record the trip. Currently, that profile appears to have various marketing / comms consents *_pre-ticked_* (i.e., ‘Promotions & Tips’, ‘Bolt’s Products’ and ‘Suggestions’). In theory, this means that passengers who do not have a formal Bolt account could be sent marketing comms by default.
* *Pre-ticked boxes or implied consent to marketing is against local laws* (!) If the business wants to send marketing communications to kiosk users, the kiosk journey would need a clear, consent box in Thai that gives riders a real choice. Otherwise, no marketing messages should be sent to those users.
* We are currently in discussions with the business to ensure that no such comms are sent to this type of Bolt user - however, if at any point the business wants to send marketing comms to them, the kiosk UI would need to include a consent box to cover this. We can assist with this if needed.

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
*Vendor Data Processing*
{panel}

* Bolt and the partner will be sharing personal data about passengers and drivers. Depending on the type of agreement entered and the nature of the data sharing, we will need to enter into either a *Data Processing Agreement* or *Data Sharing Agreement* with the partner. Without this, we are exposing Bolt to risk if the partner breaches its own privacy obligations when handling this data.
* I understand that in Malta the business is currently debating what type of agreement to use with the partner - *do we have visibility on what agreement is being used here*? If so, please provide a copy so that we can review.

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
*Contents of printed receipts / SMS comms*
{panel}

* Local law requires that printed receipts should clearly show the *fare*, the *driver and vehicle information*, and *Bolt’s support contact*. Currently, I understand that not all of this information is included.
* Additionally, local law requires *real-time tracking of the drivers* to be accessible to the passengers. 
** For passengers with a smartphone who will receive an SMS, I understand that they will be able to view the driver’s location, s this should not be an issue.
** However, if the passenger does not have a smartphone, it is unclear how real-time tracking will be possible. We are doing some additional research on this issue, and will provide you with an update soon.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Disclaimer language in the order flow*
{panel}

* Currently, the order flow allows the passenger to click a link to Bolt’s privacy notice, and states that the passenger ‘agrees’ to the privacy notice. There are two current issues here:
** If the passenger does not have a smartphone (which is possible for those using the kiosk), they will only have access to the language in the privacy notice by clicking the link - they will not have easy access once they stop using the kiosk. We must make sure the passenger has easy access to this document at all times.
** Technically, you cannot ‘agree’ to a privacy notice - it is a transparency document, not an agreement. Using the current language risks creating the impression that we are relying on consent as a legal basis (which we should not in this case).
* To the extent not already implemented, *we suggest the following changes to the order flow*:
** It should include a link directly to the correct Passenger T&Cs and Privacy Notice in Thai.
** The relevant wording should be amended to “_By booking, you agree with TapBox/Bolt’s terms_ *_and acknowledge_* _Bolt’s privacy notice”_.
** On any printed receipt, we should include the _full link_ to the privacy notice at the bottom (i.e., “_Bolt processes your personal data in accordance with its privacy notice: [HYPERLINK]_”

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Unintended disclosure of user information*
{panel}

* Passengers will have the opportunity to print off order receipts from the kiosk. These receipts will contain, in addition to a QR code, certain personal data of the passenger and their driver. If these receipts are improperly disposed of in public places, anyone would have access to the information on the receipt. This creates a risk of unintended disclosure of personal data.
* To mitigate this risk, *we suggest the following*:
** Consider offering printed receipts only if the passenger does not accept an SMS message.
** Ensure that the QR code is only valid for a limited period of time, and that not just anyone can successfully use the QR code to access the trip / driver details.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Responding to passenger requests*
{panel}

* If a passenger who has used a kiosk submits a complaint / request to Bolt regarding the trip, we must ensure we are easily able to verify the passenger and identify the trip on our side, in order to comply with local obligations.
* *Do we have visibility on how this will work operationally on our side*? It would be helpful to understand this in case we need to advise on the process.

This does not mean that this equals fraud 100%. We are protecting Bolt because this money has not been checked yet. (Hence the try again tomorrow sentence)

If there is a big chance that they would walk away with the money, then we will say sorry but too risky.

25W37: Feature is QA tested, design reviewed and PRs are now merged. Pending release (targeting app version 1.52).

+*BACKGROUND*+

* In Germany, Bolt is entering into an agreement with a debt collection services providers (in the context of a vehicle financing programme): [+*LINK*+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bMkfOQr2_T5QJOIea3k-mAas10stEBYn/edit]
** Intended to be used as a framework agreement to which other countries can in future sign adherence agreements.
** Ticket originally opened in July. I was looped in on 12 September.
* Agreement:
** Service framework agreement for debt collection between Bolt Ops OU and EOS KSI Inkasso Deutschland GmbH (i.e., services for collecting Bolt’s receivables from defaulting debtors in Germany). The latter’s standard form.
*** EOS provides a debt collection portal through which Bolt can track and manage outstanding receivables ([https://www.eos-direct.de/|https://www.eos-direct.de/|smart-link] ).
*** Bolt must provide to EOS details of the transactions underlying the relevant claim, and documents and info on the claim (to prove its legitimacy).
** For indefinite term, but can be terminated by either party with one month’s notice.
** Bolt is not permitted to transfer A9/10 GDPR data to EOS, nor German ID docs (5.11).
** Clause 7 deals with data protection.
*** EOS characterised as an independent controller, per 7.4 (as the “_degree of binding instructions enables EOS KSI to carry out its activities as a specialised legal service provider without hindrance_”) - this seems fine. Bolt is instructing EOS to enforce its legal claims, so it needs a degree of independence.
*** Clause 7.3 says EOS can use Bolt data to make reports about overdue claims - this term survives the agreement. 
*** Per Clause 7.9, both parties must ensure appropriate A32 measures (unspecified).
** No mention of indemnities. However, Bolt is doing all the sharing and the data is sensitive.
** Agreement does not explicitly require compliance with privacy laws. It is also silent on types of data being transferred, data breaches, exact security measures, transfers, audits, training etc. (i.e., contents of our DSA).

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Risk Profile = {color:#36b37e}*Low*{color} to {color:#ff991f}*Medium*{color}.
** Data to be transferred: (1) Vehicle financing contracts that are the basis of the debts; and (2) orders / invoices to be paid (which are the debt that has not been collected).
* Key documentary issues are as follows:
** (The easiest thing to do here would be to include our DSA as an Annex, rather than amend the current agreement (since it is missing basically all of the core provisions)

||*Issue*||*Description*||*Mitigation(s)*||*Priority*||
|*Indemnity*|It is essential for Bolt to have an indemnity here for any breaches / personal data incidents, given that Bolt is transferring the data and such data is sensitive. As such, a breach would leave Bolt on the hook.
However, there is no such indemnity in the Agreement.|Include the pro-Bolt indemnity in the DSA. We should push hard on this, as it is reasonable to include in the circumstances.|🔴|
|*Security standards*|Although Clause 7.9 states that EOS must implement appropriate security measures, these are not specified. Given the sensitivity of the data bing transferred, it is worth documenting these more clearly.|Include our standard DSA provisions.
Also, get InfoSec to review the agreement.|:orange_circle:|
|*Post-termination retention*|Clause 7.3 says EOS can use Bolt data to make reports about overdue claims - this term survives the agreement. It is unclear precisely what data is in scope here. This creates a risk that EOS will retain and share a disproportionate amount of Bolt data.|Clarify exactly what data is needed by EOS in this regard, and limit the provision to that data. Also, subject the provision to the general requirement about purpose limitation, via a provision in the DSA.|:orange_circle:|
|*Clarity on data processing*|The Agreement is silent on exactly what data Bolt will be sharing with EOS - it is generally good to be clear on this for data management purposes.
Also, the Agreement prohibits Bolt sending A9/10 data. This increases the importance of knowing exactly what data we are transferring here, so that we can be confident we are not breaching the Agreement.|As a first step, include the usual data processing Annex in the DSA. 
Also, amend the provision so that Bolt will use reasonable endeavours not to send SCD (and will in any event do so with an appropriate legal basis). If EOS rejects this, I will need to discuss whether there is a way of vetting this on our side.|:orange_circle:|
|*Data breach notification*|The Agreement is silent on EOS informing Bolt of relevant personal data breaches. This is important for us notwithstanding the C2C relationship, given that it is data relating to Bolt debtors, and so affected debtors would likely come after Bolt first.|Include the standard PDB provision in the DSA.|:green:|
|*Audits / DSRs / Reg Inquiries*|The Agreement is silent on audits - this is an important part of ensuring that EOS has appropriate measures in place to protect the personal data we are sending.
Also, no requirement for each Party to provide reasonable assistance to the other in responding to data subject requests, complaints, or regulatory inquiries relating to Shared Personal Data. There should be.|Include the standard provisions in the DSA.|:green:|

* Other issues:
** Depending on data sensitivity here, a LIA / DPIA may be useful. However, not currently strictly necessary.
** We should generally ensure that we are only transferring data that is strictly necessary - We should ensure we have strict controls in place on this.
** In terms of transparency, we can argue this falls under the ‘legal claims’ row.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** Do we have a general indication of what data we would be uploading to the platform? Or could it be anything?
*** If the latter, is there a way we can vet data before we send it to EOW? Otherwise we would be in breach.
** Presumably the agreement would be updated if other countries entered, since it applies specifically to Germany?
*** Which other countries / entities will be entering into the arrangement?
** Why does EOS need to retain certain data after the agreement? What data?
* Actions:
** In the Agreement: (i) incorporate the DSA; and (ii) amend provision on SCD.
** Suggest inclusion of the DSA
** Flag that InfoSec should review the counterparty.

Hey [~accountid:712020:13033e65-435c-4794-a380-e007eba7615a],

This is indeed an interesting catch you made. I do believe you’re correct that the BSN could be required as TIN equivalent under DAC7.

However, to my knowledge, DAC7 is currently not (yet) listed as a specific exception in the UAVG (Dutch GDPR) or covered by an AMvB (General Administrative Order). This means there is no explicit exemption granted yet under Dutch national law to store or process the BSN for this purpose.

Theoretically, DAC7 (as an EU Directive) should overrule conflicting national restrictions, but I’m not fully confident this applies without reservation in the case of BSN processing, given the sensitivity of the BSN and the strict position of the data authorities.

This creates a legal contradiction: DAC7 requires us to collect and report the TIN, and for Dutch individuals that TIN is the BSN. Yet, under Article 46 of the UAVG, processing the BSN remains restricted unless a specific national exemption applies, which has not yet been issued (to my knowledge).

It might be worth consulting a Dutch tax and privacy lawyer to confirm whether the current DAC7 implementation provides a sufficient legal basis for BSN processing, or whether additional legal clarification is needed.

Dear Abid,

Thank you for your message. We take all data protection-related concerns seriously and want to clarify how your rights are protected under the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

*International data transfers*

Bolt transfers personal data outside the European Economic Area where this is permitted under GDPR Articles 44-49. This means transfers are based on one of the following safeguards:

* An adequacy decision by the European Commission or
* Standard Contractual Clauses approved by the European Commission.

Consent is not the legal basis relied upon for these transfers. Instead, we ensure that each transfer mechanism provides the level of protection required by EU law, as described in Section 6 of the Global Privacy Notice for Drivers, available here: [https://bolt.eu/no-no/privacy/privacy-for-drivers/|https://bolt.eu/no-no/privacy/privacy-for-drivers/|smart-link] .

*Driver rights and controls*

As a data subject, you have the right to access, rectify, erase, restrict, or object to the processing of your personal data, and to request portability of your data under the GDPR. These rights can be exercised by submitting a request through our Data Subject Rights portal, available here: [https://bolt.eu/no-no/privacy/data-subject/|https://bolt.eu/no-no/privacy/data-subject/|smart-link]  , or via email to [+privacy@bolt.eu+|mailto:privacy@bolt.eu]. We respond to all valid data subject requests within the statutory time limits, in line with the applicable law.

*Privacy Notice updates*

GDPR requires Bolt to provide clear, accessible information about how we process personal data (Articles 12-14). This is fulfilled through our Global Privacy Notice for Drivers, which is available online here: [https://bolt.eu/no-no/privacy/privacy-for-drivers/|https://bolt.eu/no-no/privacy/privacy-for-drivers/|smart-link]  . Under law, data controllers are not required to obtain separate approval from data subjects for updated privacy notices. This is because under GDPR, privacy notices serve an informational duty rather than a consent or contractual mechanism, and therefore data controllers must inform data subjects of changes but are not legally required to obtain approval each time the privacy notice is updated.

To clarify, under applicable law, Drivers are not required to provide approval for updated privacy notices and Bolt is not legally required to suspend or delay the implementation of a notice once it has been issued. Updates are provided to keep drivers informed of current processing activities.

*Privacy Notice changes*

GDPR requires Bolt to provide clear and accessible information on how personal data is currently processed. This is achieved through updating and maintaining privacy notices. GDPR does not impose an obligation on controllers to provide version-by-version comparison tables or historical change logs. Instead, our duty is to ensure that the current privacy notice reflects our processing activities in a transparent and understandable way. * Improved transparency - we reorganised the notice and updated the language to make it clearer and easier to follow;
* Categories of personal data - we added examples of what types of data we collect and use to operate the Bolt services;
* How we use your data - we clarified the reasons we use your data and the legal bases that apply (now in an easier-to-read format);
* Data sharing - we explained who we share your data with and why;
* Retention - we added more detail about how long we keep your data.

 

We take data protection obligations seriously and aim to address all requests in line with applicable laws. To date, no unlawful processing or damages have been identified.

If you wish to exercise your rights, please contact us directly at [+privacy@bolt.eu+|mailto:privacy@bolt.eu] or through the online form available here: [https://bolt.eu/no-no/privacy/data-subject/|https://bolt.eu/no-no/privacy/data-subject/|smart-link]  . Just to clarify how we assess these cases:

Bolt is not liable if the bike was parked improperly by a customer or third party, if it was knocked over by wind or other natural causes, or if it was pushed or tampered with by someone else.

Bolt may only be liable if the bike had a defect like a broken kickstand, if it was deployed or placed in a hazardous position by our systems or staff, or if we failed to act on a known risk, like repeated reports of instability in certain conditions.

Alternative way to group data by city in SQL from Olga:


{noformat}SELECT
    city_name,
    SUM(CASE WHEN tran_row_subtype = 'rental_subscription_benefit_free_minutes' THEN sum ELSE 0 END) AS total_free_minutes,
    SUM(CASE WHEN tran_row_subtype = 'rental_subscription_benefit_free_unlock' THEN sum ELSE 0 END) AS total_free_unlocks
FROM
    commerce_finance.finance_model_pl_rentals_invoice
WHERE
    tran_row_subtype IN ('rental_subscription_benefit_free_minutes', 'rental_subscription_benefit_free_unlock')
    AND country_code = 'pt'
    and tran_date >= date('2025-08-01')
    and tran_date < date ('2025-09-01')
GROUP BY
    city_name{noformat}

Just to clarify the the terminology here for clear communications

* The *Invoice Report* includes all invoices generated for a partner within a calendar month. It is based on invoice issue dates and is used primarily for financial documentation, tax reporting, and record-keeping. This report is sent *monthly* to all registered partners.
* The *Payout Report* shows all transactions that were included in a specific partner payout. It is based on balance movements (e.g. trip payments, refunds, commissions) and is intended to help partners understand *how the payout amount was calculated*. This report is sent *weekly*, aligned with the standard weekly payout cycle, but the system also supports other payout frequencies.

More details can be found here: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COMM/pages/5627314370/Reports+for+Drive+3P+partners|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COMM/pages/5627314370/Reports+for+Drive+3P+partners|smart-link]

h2. 1. Diamond Tier Scope in Georgia

h3. Eligibility Criteria

To qualify for the *Diamond Tier*, a driver must meet the following conditions:

* *Points requirement*: Minimum of *69,800 points* (points are collected from completed orders).
* *Acceptance rate*: At least *90%*.
* *Cancellation limit*: From every 100 accepted orders, the driver can cancel *no more than 8%*.

h3. Number of Drivers & Update Frequency

* The Diamond Tier is updated *monthly*, on the *1st day of each month*.
* The *latest update* was on *September 1st*, at which point there were *1,787 drivers* in this tier.

h2. Compilation of Eligible Drivers List

* The list of eligible *Diamond Tier drivers* will be compiled *manually*.
* Data will be taken directly from the driver system based on the set criteria (points, acceptance rate, cancellation rate).

h2. Format

* The compiled list will be exported and stored in *CSV format*.
* The CSV file will include key details for each driver, such as:
** *Driver name*
** *Phone number*
** *Shortened profile link*

h2. Storage & Sharing

* The CSV file will be uploaded to the *Geonet site*.
* Once uploaded, the information will be available in Geonet to ensure that *only eligible drivers* can make *outgoing calls* through the system.



h2. 2. Profile Links – Collection and Shortening

* Profile links will be *shortened using Cuttly* [http://Cutt.ly|http://Cutt.ly|smart-link] .
* Bitly is used only for shortening links and does not store or expose the underlying data.
* This ensures that only shortened, non-sensitive URLs are shared externally with Geonet.

h2. Data Sharing and Updates

* The eligible driver list is *updated monthly* on the *1st day of each month*.
* If a driver loses Diamond Tier status, their information (phone number and link) will *not be included in the next month’s list*.
* As a result, once excluded, that driver will *no longer be able to make outgoing calls* via the system, since only uploaded numbers are authorized.

h2. Safeguards and Approval Process

* To prevent errors, there will be a *two-step verification process* before the list is uploaded:
*# *Two staff members* will cross-check the data (driver details and links).
*# A *manager will provide final approval* before upload.
* This ensures:
** No full/unshortened links are shared by mistake.
** Geonet cannot access or infer the underlying driver profile information beyond the shortened link provided.

h2. 3. Management Responsibility

* It's *managed directly by Smartly*, not by Bolt.

h2. Use of Link Shortening Services

* To avoid involvement of any U.S.-based services, [http://Cutt.ly|http://Cutt.ly|smart-link]  will be used for link shortening.
* [http://Cutt.ly|http://Cutt.ly|smart-link]  *is headquartered in Gdańsk, Poland*, and therefore no U.S.-based services are engaged in this process.

19,5% is calculation of Commission / GMVActually this not very correct, because GMV includes Booking fee, which is not subject for commission calculation.

Correct approach is to calculate: Commission / (GMV - Gross Booking fee) = 19,99% => 0,01% difference

Dar es Salaam August 2025:

GMV 8 036 106
Commission 1 565 782
Booking fee 131 004

19,5% = 1 565 782 / 8 036 105

19,99% = 1 565 782 / (8 036 105 - 154 584)

154 584 = gross booking fee when net booking fee is 131 004 (in Workday and all other report we only see net booking fee, so gross booking I got from billing records)

As a preliminary point, it seems that we will be sending potentially a lot of information to EOS KSI under this arrangement, and given that such information relates to claims and debt collection it should be considered sensitive. {panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
*Data Sharing Appendix*
{panel}

Given the sensitivity of the data transfers here, we need to have robust provisions in place to ensure that any data we are sending is kept secure, and to ensure that we are appropriately protected in case EOS KSI somehow misuses the data - currently, the contractual provisions in the Agreement are not enough for these purposes (!)

* *Indemnity*: The Agreement does not contain any sort of indemnity that protects Bolt if EOS KSI breaches its privacy obligations. It is important that we push for such an indemnity because Bolt is seemingly sending all of the data at-issue, and so would be the main party ‘on the hook’ if something were to go wrong. For example, if EOS KSI suffered a security breach and leaked the data of someone subject to a debt collection, it is foreseeable that the person would go after Bolt as the most visible entity to that person (i.e., given that Bolt is the one ultimately collecting the debt). The DSA includes such an indemnity.
* *Scope of data sharing*: It is currently unclear what precise categories of data we will be sharing with EOS KSI. Given the sensitive nature of some of this information, and the need to document data transfers internally for record-keeping purposes, we should ensure that the Agreement is clear on what data will be shared. This is particularly important given that the Agreement specifies certain categories of data that we _cannot_ share, and so we need to have a tight grip on this. Annex 1 of the Appendix has been included to address this issue. {color:#4c9aff}*Please could you / EOS KSI populate the yellow highlighted sections of Annex 1 with the relevant information*{color} (I can assist with precise drafting if needed).
* *Security Standards*: Given the sensitivity of the data being transferred, we need to ensure that EOS KSI is doing enough to keep the data secure and minimising the risk of potentially damaging data breaches. The Agreement is very light-touch on this, and so the Appendix (specifically Clause 9(b) and Annex 2) includes some specific security requirements that EOS KSI should adhere to.
* *Other key obligations*: When sharing personal data with third parties, we need to ensure we have clear obligations in place regarding flagging personal data breaches, dealing with regulatory investigations that concern both parties, etc. Otherwise, we have limited options for protecting ourselves should the counterparty refuse to cooperate in such situations. The Agreement is silent on these issues, whereas our DSA includes provisions on all of these topics.

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
*Checking EOS KSI’s security standards*
{panel}

As mentioned above, given the sensitivity of the data being transferred, we need to ensure that EOS KSI is doing enough to keep the data secure and minimising the risk of potentially damaging data breaches. This should be _proactive_ (i.e., ensuring that EOS KSI is ‘trustworthy’ regarding keeping the data secure) as well as _reactive_ (i.e., including contractual obligations that we can rely on should this go wrong, as we have done in the draft DSA).

On the proactive side, the InfoSec team should review EOS KSI and consider whether their information security practices are adequate - {color:#4c9aff}*I would therefore be grateful if you could ask someone from the InfoSec team to do this*{color} (!)  so that we can be confident that the data transfers under this arrangement are not disproportionately risky. This review will be particularly important if EOS KSI push back on some of the data security measures I have proposed in the DSA.

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
*Internal controls over the data sharing*
{panel}

As flagged earlier on this SD ticket, Clause 5(11) of the Agreement prohibits Bolt from sending certain categories of sensitive data to EOS KSI (I have suggested some amendment, but EOS KSI may push back on these). To ensure that Bolt does not accidentally put itself in breach of this provision (i.e., by sending sensitive categories of data to EOS KSI), {color:#4c9aff}*we should ensure that we have sufficient controls / internal vetting in place over the information that we will be sharing*{color} (!) 

For example, if a specific team at Bolt will be sharing information with EOS KSI, we should ensure that they are properly trained on what information they can and cannot share with EOS KSI. Alternatively, if EOS KSI will have access to any of Bolt’s internal document systems and will be able to extract the documents themselves, we should tightly control have information is made available to EOS KSI and in which folders (with redactions applied as needed), so that no sensitive data is accidentally shared. I can assist with this if needed, including what specific categories of data here are prohibited.

This is also generally necessary in the context of data minimisation, as we should be suring with EOS KSI no more personal data than is strictly necessary.

I’ve been wondering how Tesla tackled critique towards their Safety Score feature, and discovered that a while back, Tesla faced quite a bit of backlash, specifically around the Forward Collision Warning (FCW) metric. The problem was that FCWs often went off even when there wasn’t any real danger, which unfairly dragged down drivers’ Safety Scores and, in turn, inflated their insurance costs (referring to [Tesla Insurance|https://www.tesla.com/insurance]). The complaints piled up so much that a class-action lawsuit was filed, and in 2024 Tesla ended up [dropping FCW from the Safety Score formula|https://finance.yahoo.com/news/tesla-quietly-removes-controversial-feature-010000593.html].

So, regarding the launch of Driving Score in Germany, are the concerns primarily about the scoring itself, or about introducing incentives tied to it? If it’s the latter, we may have more flexibility to take a cautious approach. For example, offering only modest benefits for safe driving (less generous than in the Baltics, to protect economics) or even providing no benefits at all, focusing solely on the educational aspect of the feature

I’m also curious: would it be less risky to penalize users directly for dangerous driving events, rather than relying on a score? Similar to how we handle discouraging speeding violations

*Thiago Del Bel*  [Just now|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C07K9SHJPJ7/p1757932831385579?thread_ts=1757688059.189339&cid=C07K9SHJPJ7]

Many thanks for the comments and discussion points.

These are practical risks we have limited control over (complaints, PR exposure, scrutiny etc.) and are largely driven by the perception of the driving score. The better the perception, the lower the risks. That’s why it’s probably more sensible to continue our current strategy of maintaining a low profile, monitoring user perception, reiterating and addressing errors and edge cases.

Improving in-App comms as we’re doing goes a long way. Buffers to reduce score fluctuation by minor harsh driving incidents also help. Proper and swift resolution of edge cases the same (e.g., harsh braking to avoid an accident).

Conversely, rolling out score consequences should increase scrutiny. The more relevant they are to users, the higher the scrutiny (small benefits < good benefits < penalties).

Launching in a new country should also attract additional scrutiny. The new user base needs to get used to it. Also, each country is different, offering new challenges and learning opportunities.

Certain countries, such as Germany in my experience, are particularly sensitive to monitoring practices. Thus, I would definitely begin with a soft approach (without consequences), monitor and adjust as necessary.

{quote}would it be less risky to penalize users directly for dangerous driving events, rather than relying on a score? Similar to how we handle discouraging speeding violations{quote}

As a rule, yes. Dangerous driving events are usually more objective and easier to explain and review compared to a combination of a number of driving events forming the score.

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


The refund is successfully completed. I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

*BACKGROUND*

*What is DineOut?*

* Feature within Bolt Food app (see video)

!Screen Recording 2025-09-09 at 23.01.51 (2c239f96-ea00-4897-9821-64c787f044aa).mov|width=2160,height=1630,alt="Screen Recording 2025-09-09 at 23.01.51.mov"!

 

* Focused for Bolt Food users who want to dine at the restaurant
* Interface is almost identical to usual Home Page, etc. Difference with usual BF app:
** user cannot order menu items via app, can only pay for the order if chooses so
** order is made at the restaurant using usual restaurant menu => sales agreement is concluded at the restaurant directly between user & restaurant
* Used only by restaurants who opt-in for this. Not for stores
* *Launched in Estonia in October 13*, followed by Riga, Vilnius, Warsaw, and Bucharest (late Oct). T&Cs changes, etc for those markets available [+here+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/19_bFAAODDYmfpdOO4X_UwcO5fOubdp-Yn4IpRODe_fg/edit?tab=t.0].

*How it is used?*

* *Restaurants*
** *display discounts or cashback option* with banners within their “restaurant” profile to attract customers for specific time periods. Mainly for non-peaks hours or for lunch offers (see pic below)
** *“flat” promotions:* discounts/cashbacks would apply for the whole order, regardless whether it contains alcohol.
*** *NB!* If needed then “2-row” system can be implemented to mitigate risks related to alcohol. Meaning alcohol and other items are added separately when paying and discount/cashback only applies to sum related to non-alcoholic items
** !Screenshot 2025-09-11 at 15.27.11.png|width=50%,alt="Screenshot 2025-09-11 at 15.27.11.png"!
** *banners are generic*, i.e. not referring to any specific brand or product group (e.g. alcohol) - see video
** *promo terms*: available on the banner  (e.g. time when it is applicable) + when you click on the banner - see video
** *disclaimers:* when clicking on a banner following disclaimer would be used “_Promotions apply during specified timeframes and may not apply  to alcohol or tobacco. Only one discount applies per bill, but discounts and cashback can be combined. Venues may add a service charge and are solely responsible for applying promotions.”_
** *age checks, promo application:* waiter needs to make age checks if order contains age-restricted item. Waiter confirms promo application. Waiter makes sure that bill wouldn’t contain products for which discounts, etc are prohibited - e.g. tobacco.
 
* *Customers*
** *user account needed:* discounts/cashbacks are not available for non-users
** *customer flow*
*** Find an offer you like in the Bolt Food app.
*** Head to the restaurant, order as usual.
*** Pay using the app: enter full amount from the bill. Discount/cashback is applied automatically (see video above)
*** Show your transaction ID to the waiter to confirm the payment

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

*4 - Publicity:*The agreement lacks a publicity clause restricting the Supplier's ability to make public announcements or use Bolt's name and trademarks without prior written consent.

*5 - IP Rights (IPR):*Section 4.3 fails to assign all Bespoke IPR to Bolt and does not provide necessary licensing provisions as required by Bolt's playbook.

*6 - IP Indemnity:*The document lacks any supplier indemnity clause covering intellectual property infringement claims, which is required to protect the Customer against third-party claims.

*7 - Audit rights:*The agreement lacks an audit rights clause required to grant the Customer access to the Supplier's records and systems for compliance verification.

*8 - Limitation of Liability:*The contract does not include a specific limitation of liability clause capping the Supplier's liabilities and excluding indirect or consequential damages.

*10 - Termination for Cause:*The agreement lacks a clause allowing Bolt to unilaterally terminate for material breach, supplier insolvency, or failure to meet performance standards.

*12 - Consequences of Termination:*The agreement lacks detailed termination consequences regarding refunding prepaid charges, termination assistance, and obligations for return/destruction of Bolt Data.

*13 - Sub-contracting:*The agreement does not include provisions requiring prior written consent for subcontracting, approval of subcontractor details, and maintaining the supplier's full liability.

*14 - Force Majeure:*The document lacks a Force Majeure clause establishing rights and obligations when uncontrollable events occur.

*BACKGROUND*

*What is DineOut?*

* Feature within Bolt Food app (see video)

!Screen Recording 2025-09-09 at 23.01.51.mov|width=2160,height=1630,alt="Screen Recording 2025-09-09 at 23.01.51.mov"!

 

* Focused for Bolt Food users who want to dine at the restaurant
* Interface is almost identical to usual Home Page, etc. Difference with usual BF app:
** user cannot order menu items via app, can only pay for the order if chooses so
** order is made at the restaurant using usual restaurant menu => sales agreement is concluded at the restaurant directly between user & restaurant
* Used only by restaurants who opt-in for this. Not for stores
* *Launched in Estonia in October 13*, followed by Riga, Vilnius, Warsaw, and Bucharest (late Oct). T&Cs changes, etc for those markets available [+here+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/19_bFAAODDYmfpdOO4X_UwcO5fOubdp-Yn4IpRODe_fg/edit?tab=t.0].

*How it is used?*

* *Restaurants*
** *display discounts or cashback option* with banners within their “restaurant” profile to attract customers for specific time periods. Mainly for non-peaks hours or for lunch offers (see video above)
** *“flat” promotions:* discounts/cashbacks would apply for the whole order, regardless whether it contains alcohol.
*** *NB!* If needed then “2-row” system can be implemented to mitigate risks related to alcohol. Meaning alcohol and other items are added separately when paying and discount/cashback only applies to sum related to non-alcoholic items
** !Screenshot 2025-09-11 at 15.27.11.png|width=50%,alt="Screenshot 2025-09-11 at 15.27.11.png"!
** *banners are generic*, i.e. not referring to any specific brand or product group (e.g. alcohol) - see video
** *promo terms*: available on the banner  (e.g. time when it is applicable) + when you click on the banner - see video
** *disclaimers:* when clicking on a banner following disclaimer would be used “_Promotions apply during specified timeframes and may not apply  to alcohol or tobacco. Only one discount applies per bill, but discounts and cashback can be combined. Venues may add a service charge and are solely responsible for applying promotions.”_
** *age checks, promo application:* waiter needs to make age checks if order contains age-restricted item. Waiter confirms promo application. Waiter makes sure that bill wouldn’t contain products for which discounts, etc are prohibited - e.g. tobacco.
 
* *Customers*
** *user account needed:* discounts/cashbacks are not available for non-users
** *customer flow*
*** Find an offer you like in the Bolt Food app.
*** Head to the restaurant, order as usual.
*** Pay using the app: enter full amount from the bill. Discount/cashback is applied automatically (see video above)
*** Show your transaction ID to the waiter to confirm the payment

Hi [~accountid:712020:db5b1201-8d10-4d36-ba7f-c3ddac5e909e] 

Could you please help to obtain the proof?

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt wants to use Alphabait in the Netherlands.
** AB is a gifting and engagement tool - would allow Bolt to personalise and send digital gifts (via email, SMS or postcards with QR codes) directly to drivers, as well as analyse the impact of these initiatives on engagement.
*** Emails still sent from [bolt.eu|http://bolt.eu] domain (DNS linking).
*** Message would read: “_Thank you for your effort over the past year. Thanks to you, together we’ve helped thousands of people travel safely and comfortably. As a token of appreciation, we have a gift for you. Scan the QR code and choose a gift._”
** Bolt provides driver data to AB → AB distributes the comms in Bolt’s name to the driver (i.e., branded as Bolt messages) → Bolt receives engagement reporting data from AB.
*** *Data Bolt would be sending to AB*: Driver name, email address, and postal address (if postcards used).
*** *Data AB would be sending to Bolt*: Engagement and interaction data (e.g. whether the gift was opened/claimed)
** Approximately 10,000 emails expected to be sent here.
* We have been provided with a DPA for analysis. I have saved a local copy here: [+*LINK*+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1jC_HspYHlwSLa7obdHo17a3QRGWrBtvh6cFRxlC7XFk/edit?tab=t.0]
** Deadline for review is 23 September.
* Questions:
** *_Can we rely on the Driver data we already hold (as part of our contractual relationship) to send these communications, without additional consent?_*
*** (Preference of the business is to not rely on consent)
** *_If explicit consent is required, would the recommended setup be to invite Drivers to share their details voluntarily with Alphabait via a form?_*
** *_From a GDPR and Bolt policy perspective, what is the best approach to stay compliant while keeping the driver experience frictionless?_*

+*ANALYSIS*+

* *Electronic marketing comms*:
** Sharing name and email address should be fine. Based on legitimate interest, and covered in privacy notice.
*** Provided that the right to unsubscribe is respected, processing here is low risk.
** For email/SMS, this counts as electronic direct marketing, as it is promotional in nature. However, {color:#36b37e}*we can arguably rely on soft opt-in*{color} here:
*** Driver’s details were collected in the context of a sale (i.e., by signing the T&Cs);
*** Emails are Bolt-branded - we can argue the entity sending them is the same as the one that collected their details;
**** (NB. We should still be fine even though AB is sending the comms on our behalf as a processor - we are marketing Bolt’s service. We do the same with Infobip / Braze. We just need to {color:#4c9aff}*make sure we are not promoting AB in any way*{color}, and that the sender is Bolt)
*** Marketing relates to similar goods / services, as appears to relate to action on a specific vertical; and
*** Driver will (presumably) be given the chance to opt-out.
** We should ensure that{color:#4c9aff} *clear centralised opt-out records are maintained and shared*{color} between Bolt and AB (as we have had problems with this in the past).
* *Postal comms*:
** This is a little bit more invasive than sending electronic comms (even though e-Privacy does not bite), so worth checking if this is really needed.
** If we decide this is needed, {color:#36b37e}*we can rely on*{color}{color:#36b37e} {color}{color:#36b37e}*legitimate interest*{color} (rather than consent), provided that
*** Privacy conducts an LIA (would be beneficial generally).
*** Drivers must be able to exercise their right to object to these comms, which Bolt should respect (and we should {color:#4c9aff}*maintain a ‘do not contact’ list*{color}).
*** We should {color:#4c9aff}*include a Postfilter notice*{color} in the comms, and *check the website for users that have opted out*.
**** _“Geen reclamepost meer ontvangen? Via_ [http://www.postfilter.nl|http://www.postfilter.nl|smart-link]  _meldt u zich eenvoudig af…” / “Don't want to receive any more advertising mail? Simply unsubscribe via_ [http://www.postfilter.nl|http://www.postfilter.nl|smart-link] _…”_
**** Can trigger complaints and adverse rulings if not respected.
* *DPA review*:
** Bolt party not specified. Counterparty is Dutch entity.
** Contains A28 provisions. Reasonably robust and pro-Bolt. Specific authorisation needed for sub-processors.
** Indemnity is pro-Bolt, but could be widened.
** However, {color:#ff5630}does not list specific T/O security measures{color}.
** Annex 1 sets out processor retention periods, after which the data will be anonymised.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* QUESTIONS:
** Will we be able to access records of opt-outs via ab? How will this be recorded / synced?
** Has InfoSec reviewed AB’s security measures?
** Has the LCM team confirmed if they are ok with the retention periods?
* RESPONSES:
** *_Can we rely on the Driver data we already hold (as part of our contractual relationship) to send these communications, without additional consent?_*
*** *Electronic comms*: We can get away with not relying on consent here, provided that proper unsubscribe options are provided (and we maintain a clear opt-out register / syncing of opt-outs) and the comms are silent on AB.
*** *Postal comms*: We can get away with not relying on consent here, provided that we include proper opt-out options and respect Postfilter requirements. If this is too much of a hassle / not really needed, it may be worth sticking to electronic comms only.
** *_If explicit consent is required, would the recommended setup be to invite Drivers to share their details voluntarily with Alphabait via a form?_*
*** See above - Consent not needed.
** *_From a GDPR and Bolt policy perspective, what is the best approach to stay compliant while keeping the driver experience frictionless?_*
*** See above re advice from a marketing POV.
*** Regarding the DPA, I have provided some comments, but these are minor / not a major blocker. The only important one is the indemnity.

After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. We therefore attach a copy of the personal data responsive to your request.

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. Bolt

Hey [~accountid:712020:13033e65-435c-4794-a380-e007eba7615a],

There seems to have been a bit of a translation issue earlier. I went back to the UAVG and rechecked the wording. Article 46 does not say that the BSN must be explicitly named in the law. It requires that the processing takes place within a legal framework, meaning it must be based on a statutory requirement or an AMvB.

In that sense, DAC7 and its Dutch implementation likely provide such a framework, since they require reporting the TIN, which for Dutch individuals is the BSN. 

So while DAC7 probably offers sufficient legal grounds, it may still be worth checking this with a Dutch privacy or tax lawyer, particularly if we plan to store or use the BSN beyond the reporting requirement.

Btw do we currently report the BSN?

I’d like to challenge the need to write “NET” everywhere. 

* It muddies the UI
* It’s an internal tax term — I am not confident most everyday drivers understand “gross” vs “net” as these is not everyday language
* Uber doesn’t use it
* Every ride is net, so there’s no need to say this _every_ time. If some rides were gross, and others were net, then it would make sense to include it. But not when it’s the same word repeated for every single ride request. If we need to make it clearer, we have other channels to inform drivers about this (stories, notifications, emails). But we don’t need so much repetition. 

I’d prefer to model our approach more after Uber to keep it simpler. For example:

{quote}*£10.00* (£8.54 + £1.46 est. holiday pay){quote}

Czech Republic Gazettes Bill Amending Minimum Tax Law

The Czech Republic has gazetted a bill that amends the Law on Top-Up Taxes for Large Multinational Groups and Large Domestic Groups, which implemented the [+Minimum Taxation Directive (2022/2523)+|https://research.ibfd.org/#/doc?url=/linkresolver/static/eulaw_2022_2523_eng__td1].

For details and previous reporting, _see_ [+Senate Approves Bill Amending Minimum Tax Law (24 July 2025)+|https://research.ibfd.org/#/doc?url=/linkresolver/static/tns_2025-07-24_cz_1]. The bill extends the due date for filing tax returns for the Czech domestic top-up tax from 10 months to 22 months following the end of the tax period, and for the information return from 10 months to 15 months following the end of the tax period (18 months in case of first information returns). The bill has a retroactive effect for tax periods starting from 31 December 2023.

The full text of the bill, published in the Official Gazette on 2 September 2025 can be found [+here+|https://www.e-sbirka.cz/sb/2025/316?zalozka=text] (in Czech only).

_Note_: The same bill also implements into domestic law the requirements of the [+Accounting Directive (2023/2775)+|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir_del/2023/2775/oj] regarding the adjustment of the size criteria for micro, small, medium-sized and large undertakings.

Given the City of Toronto audit starting at the end of this week, the volume of cases we’ve already seen escalate with riders, and the likelihood that a full registered dash cam solution would take a while to implement, I’d advocate for focusing on a minimum viable product at this time.

Specifically, adding a notice of recording in-app in a way that doesn’t impede rider conversion (e.g., a disclaimer in the fare breakdown or another non-intrusive location, rather than a full alert) would allow us to be compliant across all trips regardless of driver behaviour with stickers or declarations. So this is because of a new payout system where if the driver had cash orders before the weekly payout was processed, it would automatically deduct the cash payment fees to prevent the driver’s balance from going into debt. We came to the conclusion that the best solution to ensure Bolt’s revenue and do not impact supply would be: *to adjust the driver to rider invoice to the amount compensated by Bolt to the driver.* It would br the most pragmatic solution.
If the ride was 10EUR + 2 VAT but the rider didn’t pay, Billing would need to credit note the original invoice and issue new one for 5 +1EUR
This solution is not compliant because the new document would be reported and paid in the period where taxable supply happened but this is the way how we can accommodate growing number of fiscalised markets, if we are ok with bearing this level of risk.
This solution will help us to minimalise the risk on tax treatment of the compensations and decrease the financial burdens on the driver.
Full analysis here: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1hHd9ArS0AV-Sb_C9c2uyTd5oQr1Pl_Jz8X1l6B-Y4W8/edit?tab=t.0|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1hHd9ArS0AV-Sb_C9c2uyTd5oQr1Pl_Jz8X1l6B-Y4W8/edit?tab=t.0|smart-link] 
Sample calculation here: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1p-jNhoW0XGSren-_uZ-4ywOCecXfpnaLlk0nCGfC6gc/edit?gid=0#gid=0|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1p-jNhoW0XGSren-_uZ-4ywOCecXfpnaLlk0nCGfC6gc/edit?gid=0#gid=0|smart-link] 
I hope it would also help us to standardize the process of partial payments. Currently the situation if the rider paid only *part* of the (cash) ride is as follow:

# Markets with PR enabled
## PR requested: The issue will be resolved using the paid price.
## PR not requested: No changes: the price will remain the same.
# Markets with PR disabled: No changes : the final price will remain the same regardless of the paid amount.

The issue which I see here is that price review may require human intervention and RH would like to resign from it.

Without diving into the details, based on my experience, I can tell you this.

When using dbt on Databricks, it manages Spark for you. Usually, you don't need to care about what happens inside Spark (although sometimes it is useful to understand, when looking for bottlenecks in your job).

So, most of the time when you have very strange low-level Spark errors, it is most likely that the cluster (and especially its driver node) cannot handle the load. Like when it runs out of memory, you see strange exceptions from the Spark internals.

In some uncommon cases, it can also be a bug in Databricks. We can report this to Databricks when that happens.

I hope you won'd get such errors in the future anymore :crossed_fingers::skin-tone-3: and if you do, you can check the health of the driver node and try increasing it or with a different cluster size

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

Repetitive rides with the same rider or phone number are a clear indicator of fraud, but unfortunately, there are cases where this doesn't occur. For example, some drivers create multiple rider accounts with different phone numbers to perform self-orders. These self-rides often have other distinct characteristics, such as being unusually short or having strange pick-up times and locations.

However, this type of profiling can lead to false positives, especially in new or small markets as they grow. I believe that's what happened here.

In the future, if you encounter similar cases that you suspect are false positives, please submit a ticket. We can then investigate and determine if the driver can be compensated for the lost campaign bonus.

*3 - Confidentiality:*The agreement is missing a confidentiality clause that should include a broad definition of Confidential Information, restricted disclosure, and return/destruction obligations, leaving Bolt's sensitive information unprotected.

Hey [~accountid:619cad8cb43d5b006af304cc], sharing my POV:

1. Voluntary placement / driver consent

I think that drivers can voluntarily place materials in their vehicles. In CH, there is no general prohibition against _non-commercial, informational signage_ inside a driver’s own car.

To avoid any claim of “forced advertising” or hidden working conditions, best practice is to make it _clearly voluntary_ and document opt-in (through fleet managers or HUB distribution).

For self-employed drivers, forcing placement could raise employment law questions - better to position this as optional with an incentive.



2. Required language / disclaimers / placement rules

*Content risk:*

The wording looks like basic courtesy requests. This is _low-risk_ and not treated as commercial advertising under Swiss law.

However, regulators could argue the “rules of the house” blur the line between driver as service provider vs. platform as rule-setter, so this can create risk of classification as employer. To mitigate, it should be clear that *these are driver’s personal preferences*, not Bolt’s terms of service. A small disclaimer like _“These notes reflect your driver’s personal preferences and are shared to make the ride more comfortable. They are not part of Bolt’s terms of service. Please feel free to let your driver know what works best for you.”_ or something like that could reduce risk.

*Size/placement:*

No statutory specs in CH, but local police may enforce if visibility is impaired, so placement should not block windscreen/driver’s view, ideally limited to backseat area.

*Distribution channels*

*No restriction* on using HUBs, fleets, or events to distribute. But if distributed at HUBs, messaging must clarify voluntariness. If given through fleet owners, check that fleet managers are not mandating placement (to avoid employment control angle).



If you have any other questions - please let me know, thanks!

Thank you for you comments! 

* How we send notifications to FOs (whether by email or in-app) is at our full discretion. My advice would be to: (i) send a message to all new FOs during onboarding; and (ii) send a broader informational message to all existing FOs.
* T&Cs already implicitly provide that the fleet is obliged to obtain the insurance: 
** Clause 5.5. _“You are solely responsible for ensuring that:_ +_you are lawfully able to fulfil_+ _Ride-Hailing Services; and your Appointed Drivers (if any) are lawfully able to fulfil Ride-Hailing Services on your behalf.” -_ since having a commercial liability insurance is required by law, providing taxi services without it would violate clause 5.5. 
** Clause 12.1 that states that  _“the fleet agree to_ +_indemnify and fully reimburse Bolt for_+ _any claims, losses and costs […] incurred as a result of your use of the Bolt Platform including those relating to: (i) any breach of your obligations in these Platform Terms; (i )any ownership, use, maintenance or operation of a vehicle; (i)_ +_any failure to comply with applicable laws, regulations, or industry standards by you_+_” -_ Thus, if we mention during onboarding the obligation of a Fleet to obtain the required insurance and the Fleet fails to do so, this constitutes a breach of its obligations. Therefore, an immediate update of the T&Cs is not necessary, as we are already covered. However, once the next T&C updates are implemented, we can explicitly include a reference to business liability insurance. This update is desirable but not urgent.
* Even if the insurance has not yet been finalised at the time when the car is created in the system, the notification during the onboarding must clearly state that it is the Fleet’s obligation to apply for business liability insurance before taxi services are provided. If the Fleet has already applied for the insurance but the policy has not yet been physically issued, it may start providing services only if it is confident that the insurance will retroactively cover the taxi service period. The Fleet must provide Bolt with a copy of the policy immediately upon receipt, but in any case no later than one (1) business day thereafter.

Consider various breaking change scenarios and their corresponding deployment implications:

* *Fatal Breaking Changes:* Changes that should explicitly _block_ deployment.
** Example: Changing the data type of an existing field in a request or response (e.g., from string to integer) for a mandatory field. This implies immediate client incompatibility.
* *Order-Dependent Breaking Changes:* Changes that require packages to be deployed in a specific sequence.
** Example: Removing a mandatory field from a request or response. This necessitates deploying the producer and consumer services in a specific order to avoid runtime errors.
** Example: Adding a new mandatory field to a request.
* *Non-Breaking Changes:* Changes where deployment order is not critical.
** Example: Adding an optional field to a request or response.
** Example: Adding a new optional API endpoint.

{code:sql}WITH retry_recovery AS (
WITH initial_failed AS (
SELECT DISTINCT 
co.payment_order_id 
FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders co
WHERE co.created_date BETWEEN date '2025-04-01' AND date '2025-06-30'
AND co.order_type = 'rides'
AND co.is_initial_failed_payment
GROUP BY 1 
)
SELECT DISTINCT 
co.order_id,
co.city_id
FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders co 
JOIN ng_public.etl_fraud_payments_data p ON p.id = co.id 
JOIN initial_failed ifp ON ifp.payment_order_id = co.payment_order_id 
WHERE co.created_date BETWEEN date '2025-04-01' AND date '2025-06-30'
AND p.created_date BETWEEN date '2025-04-01' AND date '2025-06-30'
AND (p.count_payments > 1 OR p.count_capture_attempts > 1)
AND co.is_current_failed_payment = FALSE
AND co.last_payment_row_state = 'finished'
),
refund_recovery AS (
SELECT DISTINCT 
co.order_id,
co.city_id
FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders co
WHERE co.created_date BETWEEN date '2025-04-01' AND date '2025-06-30'
AND co.order_type = 'rides'
AND co.is_initial_failed_payment 
AND co.refund_amount >= co.initial_failed_payment_amount 
)
SELECT 
month(co.created) AS MONTH, 
CASE WHEN rr.order_id IS NOT NULL THEN 'retry_recovery' WHEN re.order_id IS NOT NULL AND rr.order_id IS NULL THEN 'refund_recovery' ELSE 'user recovery (top up or next order)' END AS recovery_method,
SUM(co.user_price_eur) AS sum_user_price_eur,
COUNT(DISTINCT co.id) AS count_orders,
ROUND(CAST(SUM(co.uncovered_amount/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),2) AS fp_sum,
ROUND(CAST(SUM(co.initial_failed_payment_amount/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),2) AS initial_fp_sum
FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders co
LEFT JOIN retry_recovery rr ON rr.order_id = co.order_id AND rr.city_id = co.city_id
LEFT JOIN refund_recovery re ON re.order_id = co.order_id AND re.city_id = co.city_id
WHERE co.created_date BETWEEN date '2025-04-01' AND date '2025-06-30'
AND co.order_type = 'rides'
AND co.order_state = 'finished'
AND (co.initial_failed_payment_amount > 0 OR co.is_initial_failed_payment)
AND co.uncovered_amount = 0
--AND (CASE WHEN COALESCE(co.card_booked_amount,0) > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0 -- with/without preauth
--AND COALESCE(co.card_booked_amount,0) > 0 -- with preauth, to check price increases
--AND co.user_price <= co.booking_amount_total -- without price increase
--AND co.user_price > co.booking_amount_total -- with price increase
GROUP BY 1,2
ORDER BY 1 DESC,2{code}

Thank you for your inquiry which we received on *29 August 2025* about sharing of your personal data with third parties. Sharing data with these partners allows us to provide you with a seamless experience, ensuring the reliability and functionality of our services.

 

We share data with independent data controllers (such as drivers or couriers), or law enforcement authorities to facilitate smooth operations, ensure safety and security, and comply with legal obligations. Our data sharing practices undergo thorough evaluation to ensure that they are justified by a legitimate legal basis and align with privacy regulations.

 

We take the responsibility of sharing your personal data very seriously. Bolt is entitled to share your personal data if the data sharing is necessary for providing services to you, complying with Bolt’s legal obligations, or pursuing its legitimate interests or a third party. 

 

To ensure that your data is protected, we implement necessary safeguards. This includes the assessment of data protection and security practices of the data recipients and, when your data is transferred outside the EEA, conclusion of Standard Contractual Clauses (SCC) approved by the European Commission, available at: [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dec_impl/2021/914/oj|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dec_impl/2021/914/oj|smart-link] . If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

~ Summary of the call ~

h2. *Project Context*

* *Initiative origin:* Samira (BD manager, ex-doctor) proposed an ambulance service on Bolt platform. Idea transferred to ride-hailing team, led by Farid.
* *Current stage:* Planning phase. Legal has not raised blockers; privacy considerations under review.

----

h2. *Operational Model*

* New *“Ambulance” category* in Bolt app.
* Users can order an ambulance to private hospitals for transfer, first aid, or consultation.
* *Process flow:*
*# User selects ambulance in app.
*# Pop-up disclaimer informs Bolt is not liable, service provided by third party.
*# Order dispatched to ~40 private hospital ambulances via service provider.
*# Medical consultant (not Bolt) may call patient pre-arrival to advise or escalate to public ambulance if critical.
*# Ambulance provides care/transfer to hospital.
* *Motivation:* Public ambulances in Baku unreliable (40–60 min wait or none). Private hospital ambulances underutilized.
* *Service provider:* Acts as intermediary, contracts with hospitals, runs call centre, assumes operational liability. Bolt’s role limited to dispatch & sharing location data.

----

h2. *Privacy & Legal Discussion*

* *Aleksander (privacy):*
** Bolt must avoid collecting or handling medical data.
** Must clarify in pop-ups and disclaimers that Bolt is only a facilitator.
** Personal data sharing limited to location + basic ride details.
** A *Data Sharing Agreement (DSA)* needed alongside commercial contract. Must ensure liability is on service provider/hospitals.
** Strong disclaimers to avoid perception Bolt stores/uses health info.
* *Next steps:* Aleks to draft privacy position in ticket; review Azerbaijani law; consider contract templates (possibly from firefighter project precedent).

----

h2. *Contracts & Responsibilities*

* Bolt contracts *only with service provider*, not hospitals directly.
* Provider contracts separately with hospitals.
* Hospitals own ambulances and employ medical staff.
* Liability chain: Bolt → Service provider → Hospitals.

----

h2. *Alignment & Next Steps*

* André emphasized project is *not exploratory but execution stage*. Team eager to launch.
* Farid confirmed service provider finalizing hospital contracts, requests template from Bolt.
* Agreement templates and DSAs need to be created from scratch.

----

h2. *Other Business (end of call)*

* Discussion shifted to *Fairmont hotel project*: CEO’s upcoming stay, showcasing Bolt cars at hotel, fixed pricing, receipts for foreign guests, need for one-pager and PR alignment.
* Coordination with PR/marketing ongoing, focus on presentation and Looker reporting setup.

The agreement should therefore include strong liability and indemnity provisions.

*3 - Confidentiality:*Section 7 lacks a broad definition of Confidential Information and omits critical provisions including purpose-limited use, standard exceptions, compelled disclosure procedures, and return/destruction obligations with certification.

*4 - IP Rights (IPR):*Clause 5 only grants an exclusive license rather than assigning all bespoke intellectual property rights to Bolt as required, preventing Bolt from having full ownership of bespoke outputs.

*5 - IP Indemnity:*Clause 10 lacks provisions for supplier control of the defense and remedial actions in the event of an infringement claim, limiting Bolt's protection against IP infringement risks.

*6 - Audit rights:*The agreement is missing a required audit rights provision that would ensure full, transparent record keeping and access for Bolt to verify compliance.

*7 - Limitation of Liability:*Clause 9 fails to establish a defined cap on the Agency's liability and does not exclude indirect, consequential, or special losses as required by our guidelines.

*8 - Standard Indemnity:*Clause 10 is overly broad, not limited to material breach, not subject to Bolt's fixed liability cap, and missing supplier mitigation and prompt notice obligations.

*9 - Termination for Cause:*Clause 4 lacks a 30-day cure period for material breaches and does not address supplier insolvency, performance failures, or non-payment issues as required.

*10 - Termination for Convenience:*Clause 4.2 improperly requires a "justified reason" and mandates termination compensation, limiting Bolt's ability to terminate for convenience without liability.

*11 - Consequences of Termination:*The Agreement fails to address key termination consequences including refund of prepaid fees, termination assistance, and procedures for return/destruction of Bolt Data.

*12 - Sub-contracting:*The Agreement lacks provisions regarding subcontracting, missing requirements for Bolt's prior written consent and disclosure of subcontractor details.

*13 - Force Majeure:*Clause 8 does not properly distinguish supplier non-performance, lacks a trigger for cumulative delays, and fails to grant Bolt rights to suspend obligations or engage third parties.

*14 - Dispute Resolution:*Clause 13.2 lacks a detailed staged process with defined escalation and mediation steps, and does not mandate continued performance during disputes.

When advising the business on the DQO feature, the most important step is this: ask the team to speak to Josef Kurchishvili and ensure proper testing is carried out before launch. We cannot form a privacy position without test data showing whether DQO materially impacts driver earnings.

+*Main points*+

* DQO potentially falls within the scope of automated decision making (ADM).
* ADM is prohibited when it has a significant effect on individuals (here, drivers) and is made without meaningful human review.
* For drivers, “significant effect” typically means a substantial drop in earnings. As a working threshold, assume a 25% or greater drop in earnings is a strong indicator of significant effect.

+*How I’d advise the business to proceed*+

# *Direct them to Josef*: Make sure they understand testing is a very important first step. Without his testing, we cannot advise on compliance.
# *What do we need them to test*:
#* If tests show drivers do not lose a significant amount of trips or earnings (below the 25% threshold), then we can argue DQO is outside the scope of prohibited ADM and proceed with launch.
#* If tests show significant loss (≥25%), the feature should not be launched in that market/shall be discussed further on how to de-risk.
#* Test results will tell us if this is ADM or not.
# *Check per market*: DQO’s effect may differ by country or city. Always ask for the latest test results per market before greenlighting launch.
# *Position with the business*: Be clear that Privacy is not blocking by default. We enable launch where data supports no significant effect. But where data indicates otherwise, the risk of breaching GDPR is high so we might need to discuss further.

+*_Summary_*+

* Testing first is critical.
* <25% earnings impact → launch possible.
* ≥25% earnings impact → do not launch - need to re-think

P.s. ask them to run this past product legal, as it might be high risk from their side (due to reclass risks)
