*Question No 8:* *Please describe whether and how recurring problems arising from consumer complaints are collected and analyzed, and how they are used to improve the service.*

We have the Customer Experience organisation run by @fred.gehrke to take care of this. For each verticals we have dedicated Program Managers and Insights Managers (analysts) to support. Mainly this would be done in two ways:

# Analysing most common contact reasons 
Each request from a user will have an issue type that would explain for what purpose they’re contacting our CS team.
Insights Managers analyse issue types with highest volumes of requests to identify gaps / process improvements
Program Managers are provided the analysis and can work with the dedicated Process Designers in CS to make improvements
# Analysing customer satisfaction
Every time a user contacts CS through the app, they can rate their experience from 1-5 at the end with feedback
Insights Managers analyse the lowest ratings (3-5) to identify gaps / process improvements
Program Managers are provided the analysis and can work with the dedicated Process Designers in CS to make procedural improvements or liaise with the CS-Operations org with concerns over quality / training

*Question No 10:* *Please explain what changes have been made to the customer service and complaint resolution system over the last 12 months.*

So, there isn’t really one very good and simple answer here. Therefore, I would emphasize first and foremost that:
“As can be seen from the earlier description (referring to the explanation I shared above, i.e., question no. 8), the focus is on the continuous improvement of processes. Bolt has approximately 2,500 customer support processes in use at the global level, covering both specific and more general situations. Changes in customer support processes may stem from consumer, partner, and courier partner complaints or feedback, as well as from platform development or the streamlining of internal processes. Since root causes are continuously analyzed and improvements are made on an ongoing basis—whether larger or smaller changes—it is difficult to point to one specific cause that has driven changes globally or in Estonia over the past 12 months.”

*Question No 1: Please submit Bolt Operations OÜ's standard terms and conditions that apply to contracts concluded with consumers and regulate the complaint resolution procedure.*

Standard Terms and Conditions (“T&Cs”) that apply to consumers using Bolt Food platform are available on Bolt’s webpage under the legal section where users need to select the relevant country where it uses the platform. Estonian consumer T&Cs are available in Estonian here and English here. 

Bolt Operations OÜ, which operates the Bolt Food platform, is not the seller of the goods offered on the platform nor the provider of the delivery services. As such, Bolt does not bear a legal obligation to resolve consumer complaints or to issue refunds in relation to the quality of the purchased goods or the delivery services, which are provided by independent third-party merchants and delivery partners.

Nevertheless, in order to ensure a positive user experience, Bolt takes an active role in facilitating an amicable resolution when issues arise with the goods or their delivery. In certain cases, where Bolt has reasonable grounds to believe that a consumer complaint is justified, Bolt may provide a refund in respect of the affected order. To assess the matter, Bolt may request further information or supporting evidence from the consumer, such as photographs or other details, which are then compared with information obtained from the merchant or the delivery partner.

If a consumer is dissatisfied with Bolt’s proposed resolution, or if they wish to address the matter directly, they are encouraged to contact the merchant or the delivery partner themselves. Merchant contact details (such as email and telephone number) are always available in the merchant’s profile on the Bolt Food platform. With regard to delivery partners, consumers are able to contact the partner directly through the application during an active order by using the dedicated contact function visible under the active order screen.

If a consumer wishes to contact a delivery partner after the order has been delivered, cancelled, or otherwise concluded, they may find the delivery partner’s full name on the fiscal receipt sent by email. Should additional contact details be required, the consumer can request these from Bolt’s customer support. Above is also reflected in consumer T&Cs under section 5. 

Clear and simple instructions how to act or how to contact merchant, delivery partner or Bolt CS in case of standard issues or any other issues are also easily findable in the Bolt Food app if the user opens up the Support section and Help Articles under his Profile.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt wants to enable data API integration for fleets in London (as is done for fleets in other markets).
** Integration allows data on the fleet portal to be _automatically_ transferred to the fleet (rather than needing to be downloaded manually). 
*** Most of this data is already accessible to the fleet via the portal - however, integration provides enhanced visibility on certain elements (booking fees and commission rates, which are not on the portal) - see [here|https://apidocs.bolt.eu/fleetIntegration/fleetIntegrationGatewayAuth/#/public-api-doc/fleetIntegrationV1GetFleetOrders] for list of all datapoints.
** We previously advised on making the data available for Odysse on [+LSS-51181+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/jira/servicedesk/projects/LSS/issue/LSS-51181]. The integration would _automatically_ transfer all of this data. 
*** I previously advised that data sharing with Odysse was fine - Main concerns were with sharing data on performance (due to bias and reclass risk - does not apply to fleet drivers) and showing gross earnings (Legal prefers showing net earnings, due to transparency around effective pay and potential wage equivalence concerns - conclusion was we can show both if it is only visible to the fleet and Bolt is not using it to influence drivers).
** Slack thread is here: [LINK|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C02N479PM9T/p1757926775485619]
* Business is asking if we can enable to integration for Odysse and any acquired fleets moving forward.

+*THOUGHTS*+

* Data visible to the fleet on the fleet portal is [here|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/~63abfbe56ad11358a0986246/pages/6183125540/Fleet+Portal+-+Available+Data+for+Fleet+Owners]. Effectively matches the list provided on this ticket.

** Checking the [link|https://apidocs.bolt.eu/fleetIntegration/fleetIntegrationGatewayAuth/#/public-api-doc/fleetIntegrationV1GetFleetOrders], only additional categories are waiting time and account status (e.g., blocked), which is fine (but check suspension reason).

+*NEXT STEPS*+

** What do we mean by ‘automatic’ transfers here? Not a blocker, I am just not fully clear on what is new here.
** Is [this|https://apidocs.bolt.eu/fleetIntegration/fleetIntegrationGatewayAuth/#/public-api-doc/fleetIntegrationV1GetFleetOrders] the full data list, under ‘Schemas’? If so, what ‘suspension reason’ is shown (_FleetIntegration.GetFleetDriversResponse_)?

Hi [~accountid:712020:ae577659-94ad-4dbe-8521-60c88964fb11] , 

Thanks for escalating. From my understanding of this situation, the question to the Privacy team whether anything further can be shared with the passenger about actions taken against the driver. Do not hesitate to let me know if this is not the reason why this ticket was raised with Privacy, or if you are needing a different kind of input.

From a privacy perspective, we must refrain from disclosing personal data of third parties, including any disciplinary measures or account actions taken against a driver. Under GDPR, “personal data” is any information relating to an identified or identifiable person, which also includes whether their account was suspended, warned, or subject to other actions. Disclosing this information to the passenger would therefore mean unlawfully sharing the driver’s personal data with someone who has no legal right to receive it.

The approach you have followed so far has been correct: you already confirmed to the rider that we cannot share specific actions, but that appropriate measures were taken. If the passenger continues to insist, you can carefully elaborate along these lines:

* Acknowledge her experience and reassure her that we take such matters very seriously.
* Emphasise that we contacted the driver and took measures to ensure this does not happen again.
* Clarify that while we cannot disclose the details of those measures due to data protection law, the case was investigated thoroughly and addressed in line with our internal safety procedures. We cannot share personal or disciplinary details about another individual, even when the concern is justified. 
* Reassure her that her report directly contributed to the actions we have taken.

This way, the rider understands that our limits are not because we want to be opaque, but because the law obliges us to protect the driver’s personal data as much as the passenger’s personal data.

Hi Laura,

Thanks for sharing the Proposal. I’ve reviewed the T&Cs and added my mark-ups (linked [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1gDuzMCH32y2NuTmFPGUiQVOZmHKa0-yXTxr_qAssUPw/edit?usp=drive_link]). A few important points are missing that normally help protect Bolt, so before I make further changes, could you confirm the following for me:

# *Payment timing* – Clause 1.3 of the T&Cs say we need to pay the full balance 30 days before the event (after paying the deposit). Is 30 days okay with you?
# *Services included* – Page 4 of the Proposal lists the services included. Can you confirm these cover everything we need/expect?
# *Price* – The Proposal sets the cost at *£25,300 for 80 guests*, plus *£316.25 for each extra guest*. VAT will be added on top. Is the business happy with this pricing?
# *Minimum guests* – The minimum charge (set out on page 4 of the Proposal) is for 80 guests (£25,300), and extra guests are £316.25 each, plus VAT. Are we happy to commit to this amount of people and payment structure?
# *Payment plan* – In clause 3.1 of the T&Cs, they ask for *75% upfront (non-refundable)*, with the balance due 30 days before the event. Are we okay with this?
# *Credit card surcharge* – In clause 3.4 of the T&Cs, they add a *2% fee if we pay by credit card*. Do we expect to pay by credit card? If so, we may want to push back on this.
# *Cancellation costs* – Clause 4.4 of the T&Cs provides that if we cancel, we’d still need to pay at least *87.5% of the full cost (£22,137.50, plus VAT/additional guests)*. Is the business comfortable with this risk?
# *Event restrictions* – Page 6 of the Proposal says we need written approval from the Event Manager if we want to bring in entertainment, accessories, or hires not on their approved list. Are we okay with this restriction?
# *Liability cap* – Their liability is limited to what we pay them (~£25,300). So, for example, if something went wrong and a guest got injured due to their negligence, that’s the max they’d cover. Is the business okay with this limit?
# *Insurance* – Their insurance does *not* include personal accident cover. This means if a guest has an accident at the event that isn’t directly caused by Evolve’s negligence, they would *not* be covered by Evolve’s insurance. In practice, guests would need to rely on their own personal insurance, or potentially look to Bolt if they feel we should be responsible. Essentially, there’s no safety net for “general accidents,” only for incidents where Evolve is proven to be at fault (and even then, their liability is capped at £25,300 as noted above). Are we happy to proceed without this?



Let me know if you’d like to discuss any of these points or the mark-ups — happy to walk you through them.

Thank you in advance! 🙂

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt wants to send a questionnaire to drivers in the Netherlands to gather insights ([link|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1eNzMfmUTbtcoRco2bd-6BQTIWxRlcF-GvSow2aVkMwI/edit?tab=t.0]).
** Qs will collect the categories of data listed in he ticket description.
* By sharing feedback, drivers enter into the chance of winning a EUR 100 voucher.
* *Request*: Review the Qs and confirm any issues.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Survey:
** Privacy notice link is broken.
*** Legal basis = Legitimate interest (not promotional material that would need consent). Covered in driver PN.
*** [+https://bolt.eu/nl-nl/privacy/privacy-policy-for-drivers/?category=rides+|https://bolt.eu/nl-nl/privacy/privacy-policy-for-drivers/?category=rides] is a broken link. Should be [https://bolt.eu/nl-nl/privacy/|https://bolt.eu/nl-nl/privacy/privacy-for-drivers/?category=rides][*privacy*|https://bolt.eu/nl-nl/privacy/privacy-for-drivers/?category=rides][-for-drivers/?category=rides|https://bolt.eu/nl-nl/privacy/privacy-for-drivers/?category=rides] 
** Questions:
*** Email address (to contact user if they have won the prize) - Fine.
*** How long driving with ride-hailing apps - Fine.
*** Why they chose to use ride-hailing apps - Fine.
*** Do they use other apps - Fine.
*** What other work do they do - Ok, but “Other employment” option may imply an employment relationship with Bolt.
*** Estimated percentage distribution of turnover across various elements of the app - Fine, but check with Regional Legal.
*** What other channels do they receive rides from - Fine.
*** Number of hours / trips per week - Fine.
*** Are they happy with Bolt - Fine.
*** Do they have accident insurance/ Do they contribute to pension scheme - Fine.
*** What could be done to improve - Ok, but some suggesting are having a fixed work schedule and driving exclusively for one app. Worth checking we are not implying an employment relationship here.
*** Type of vehicle and vehicle financing - Fine.
*** Caregiving responsibilities - Ok, provided that options are kept as they are (i.e., strictly yes / no).
** We should ensure that data is retained for no longer than is necessary. Generally, 6 months works.
* Deciding on the winner:
** Separate to the general survey results, we are also processing the driver’s data for the purpose of selecting a winner. We can only do so based on contractual necessity if there is a contract. Also, generally helpful for transparency and clarity.
*** Generally, we rely on [this doc|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ybRlet8ae-IPsv5T7MemwjSEYiNGi0afYS5DQS3Nzb8/edit?tab=t.0], but Regional legal should be consulted.
* Reaching out to the winner:
** We inform the driver in the survey that their email will be used to contact them about the prize, so this is fine.
** It is unclear how we will be sending the prize to the driver - if this is also via email, then this is fine. If we subsequently ask for further info to send them the prize, I will need to consider this.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** What insights are we trying to gather here? Why does Bolt need this data / what initiative is this part of?
** How is the winner selected - is this at random? Is this governed by the usual T&Cs?
** What will the contact to the winner look like? Will we be asking for additional data to send them the prize?
* Advice:
** Survey Qs look fine, subject to the following:
*** Include correct privacy notice link.
*** Ensure that the caregiving question (Q36) is no more granular than it already is.
** There should ideally be a set of T&Cs governing this, which should be appended or linked.
* Loop in Regional Legal 
** Get their views on whether any of the Qs create reclass risk (should be fine, but just to check), i.e.,:
*** Q5 - Other work is “Other employment”
*** Q18 - Improvements as driving exclusively for one app and having fixed hours.
** What T&Cs should we use for the giveaway?

*Attendance Note*

*Location:* Teams Meeting 
*Date:* 16 September 2025 

*Time:* 10am 
*Attendees:*

* *Lambeth:* Elliot Quinn, John Roberts 
* *Bolt:* Giulio del Balzo di Caprigliano, Daisha Ferdinand, Catherine Owlett 

+*Key Discussion Points*+

*1. Tier System and Fleet Progression*

* The council confirmed the *tier system is non-negotiable*.
* Progression between tiers involves *doubling of fleet size*. Reviews will be linked to bay installations. Initial fleet size is in the MOU but subject to *annual review*.
* Council expects *100–150 bay locations installed*, leading to a “decent fleet jump”.
* Elliot stressed concern that Bolt and similar operators could *deploy large fleets (e.g. 3,000 bikes) quickly*, clogging streets. He noted Bolt entered the market later than others, but this was not the council’s concern.

*2. Compliance vs Utilisation*

* Giulio suggested focusing tier progression on *compliance, not utilisation*.
* Elliot raised enforcement challenges: although bikes must be parked in bays, *exceptions (e.g. dropped curbs)* are tolerated. Compliance monitoring is partly reliant on operator apps.
* Examples cited:
** Kensington & Chelsea experience where *operators moved bikes despite correct user parking*.
** Resident complaints often *misidentify operators*, complicating tracking.

*3. Complaints and Reporting Tools*

* Proposals included:
** Council-run *web form/email portal* for residents to report compliance issues (with photo evidence).
** Adoption of *K&C’s performance tool* or a *common reporting system* (as used in Germany) for consistency across operators.
* General agreement that a common system would reduce council burden.

*4. Excess Fleet Capacity and Fines*

* Discussion on fines linked to fleet caps:
** *Council concern:* lower-tier operators may treat fines as a “nominal charge” and exceed caps.
** Giulio noted higher-tier operators could absorb fines more easily, so *responsibility should scale with fleet size*.
** Elliot and John will review how to structure penalties to avoid *disincentivising compliance* at Tier 1 while ensuring Tier 3 cannot abuse the system.

*5. Data Sharing and Monitoring*

* Council intends to use *live data dashboards* for fleet monitoring. Lime’s separate system may be integrated via API.
* Giulio recommended council retain *audit rights* to verify data accuracy. Elliot confirmed this would be considered in the next MOU iteration.
* Council acknowledged *progress with incumbent operators* but flagged challenges with universal adoption of Bluesystems.

*6. Cross-Borough Trips*

* Giulio raised issue of *users finishing rides outside boroughs* (currently <5 cases per day).
* Council preference: allow parking in bays but disable *re-hire in Lambeth*, with operators responsible for rebalancing.
* Agreed volumes are low, but operators must *ensure compliance with bay parking*.
* Council to share updated bay maps (last updated Aug 2025).

*7. Timelines and Next Steps*

* Council aims to finalise the MOU *before Christmas (target October)*, subject to political sign-off. Dockless bikes are politically sensitive.
* Giulio flagged Bolt’s Senior Executive will be meeting London boroughs to build relationships; potential further meeting suggested.
* Council confirmed that Bolt will have sight of a V3 of the MOU prior to any sign-off. 
* Council and Bolt to continue discussions on:
** Finalisation of reporting tools and fines.
** Data-sharing specifications and audit rights.
** Updated bay maps and integration.

If you need a *report*, please refer to FleetX (DriverX). If your request concerns an *invoice*, follow these steps:

   * If you encounter any other error, please let us know.
5. Commission invoices for the entire history of the fleet/driver are available either under **Invoice tasks** or **Partner Invoices**.

The core of this project is sending *anonymized driver profile links* to our call center partner, Geonet. We are taking comprehensive measures to ensure data security and privacy:

* *No Data Exposure:* Geonet employees will not have access to any personal data. They will only see shortened, non-descriptive links.
* *Strict Access Control:* The links require special security certificates and can only be opened by our company’s certified employees, which means no other third party can access them.
* *Anonymization:* We will use a link-shortening tool to ensure that Geonet cannot see the names of our internal systems, such as “admin.”

This method is highly secure and preferable as it protects us from having to directly share sensitive driver identifiers (e.g., IDs, personal codes) and eliminates the need for further NDAs or related agreements.

Hi [~accountid:61693adebfa2c1006b54684f] ,

Many thanks for the clarifications you provided. After reviewing this project and discussing it internally, we unfortunately cannot approve it from a privacy perspective at this point in time.

The main concerns we identified are as follows:

* *Exposure of Admin links*: A URL shortener only masks the link until it is clicked. Should anyone at Geonet (or a third-party who get access to the file) click the shortened link, the browser still will attempt to resolve and display the full original URL in the address bar. Even if they don’t have the right certificates or credentials to actually open Admin, the internal structure of the Admin URL (including references to “admin” and the driver’s identifier string) will be exposed. That in itself counts as a disclosure of internal system information and of personal data (since the URL contains a direct pointer to an individual driver’s profile).
* *Use of external link shorteners*: The proposal relies on Cuttly. While the company is Polish, its infrastructure uses US-based sub-processors (Cloudflare, analytics, etc.). This leads to unnecessary external processing and the risk of international transfers.
* *No clear necessity*: From a data minimisation perspective, the same business objective (direct support for Diamond Tier drivers) could be achieved without exposing internal identifiers or creating additional transfers of driver data.

Given these issues, the project in its current form is not compatible with our data protection obligations and the heightened regulatory environment in Georgia.

If any other initiatives come up in the future, we’d be happy to help assess them from a privacy perspective.

Hi team, 

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount. 


Please let me know if you have any other questions.

Cheers,
Afiba

Hi Team,

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

Many thanks for your feedback. We have also had a discussion and reviewed our approach from a legal standpoint, specifically regarding its compliance with local legislation.

Our main goal was to address two key issues simultaneously:

# Do not share any personal data. The new process had to be designed so that no personal information is ever disclosed to Geonet.
# Avoid sharing the administrative links themselves. Our aim was to prevent the exposure of the admin panel's name, or any part of its internal structure, at any point during the process.

This is what we took into consideration when we designed the process. We have explored a solution to prevent the exposure of any personal data, including the unique link itself. For an uncertified user, the link appears as follows:

{{https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fleet-root/partners/edit/2969019?tab=partner_profile&filte[…]2offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Asia%2FTbilisi}}

As we see this link does not contain any personal data in its name (please clarify if something is wrong). When a user without the proper certificate attempts to access it, the system displays an error, preventing them from viewing any information.

!Screenshot 2025-09-17 at 13.00.32.png|width=571,height=352,alt="Screenshot 2025-09-17 at 13.00.32.png"!

Even though the links didn't contain personal data, our aim was to prevent the exposure of the admin panel's name or any part of its internal structure at any point during the process.

Accordingly, our operations team found a URL shortener that would address this. The shortened link would appear as follows:

{{https://shorturl.at/hMcLq}}

!Screenshot 2025-09-17 at 13.01.22.png|width=685,height=40,alt="Screenshot 2025-09-17 at 13.01.22.png"!

When a user clicks on this shortened link, two key things happen:

* The browser *does not resolve to the full, original URL* in the address bar.
* The system *does not open the link's content* and instead displays an error.

!Screenshot 2025-09-17 at 13.00.56.png|width=571,height=352,alt="Screenshot 2025-09-17 at 13.00.56.png"!



h3. *Clarification on International Data Transfers*

Regarding the concern about international data transfers to a US-based sub-processor, we have reviewed this in accordance with Georgian legislation.

International data transfer cases in Georgia require a platform application to be submitted to the State Inspector's Service, where we must specify exactly what personal data is being transferred to a non-European country, such as the United States.

However, this requirement does not apply to our situation because *we are not transferring any personal data.* As we've outlined, the entire process is designed to prevent the disclosure of any personal data.

In practice, a company is only required to submit an application for international data transfer if they are providing information that contains personal data. Since no personal data is involved in this process, we believe it falls outside the scope of that regulation.

To summarize, we are confident in our approach because:

# The link itself does not contain any personal data.
# After the shortened link is clicked, the user sees an error page and the original URL is not exposed.
# No third party will be able to see any personal data or even the name of our internal platform ("admin").

I also want to agree with your point regarding *data minimization*. While we understand that the business objective could potentially be achieved through other means, the driver for this specific solution is rooted in market competition and a clear demand from our drivers.

Our understanding is that competitor companies are already using similar features in the market. Drivers regularly communicate with each other and have expressed a strong desire for this kind of direct call center support from Bolt. Therefore, implementing this feature is a crucial step for our operations team to maintain a strong competitive position.

I also wanted to ask if we might be missing anything on the technical side. If a link were to contain personal information itself, could you please show us an example? It's clearly not in our interest to expose any data, and we want to ensure the system is as secure as possible.

Thanks,

Hi [~accountid:712020:d3a996fa-c232-493f-9fae-c2a83b486902], thanks for the clarifications! Allow me to address your points below:

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
# Personal data in Admin links
{panel}

* In the example link you provided: {{https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fleet-root/partners/edit/2969019?tab=partner_profile&filte[…]2offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Asia%2FTbilisi}}, the driver’s *partner ID* appears. It is the number that shows after the /edit/ in the link, in this specific case: {{2969019}}
* Drivers’ partner IDs are personal data, as they are unique identifiers assigned to each driver. A partner ID is sufficient to directly identify a driver, and under GDPR as well as our own Driver Privacy Notice, identifiers of this kind are treated as personal data.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
# On the use of URL shorteners
{panel}

* When the project was first presented, [https://cutt.ly/en|https://cutt.ly/en|smart-link]  was indicated as the URL shortener to be used, whereas your latest answer refers to [https://www.shorturl.at/|https://www.shorturl.at/|smart-link] , which appears to be a different service. Regardless of which service is selected, the same concerns apply about external shorteners, so the choice of provider is unlikely to change our assessment.
* I tested the shortened URL you included in your answer on two devices *without* the necessary certificates to access Admin. In both cases I was redirected to Bolt’s error page (same as in your first screenshot), and the browser resolved the shortened link to the *full original Admin URL* in the address bar. I did not receive the “Short URL error page” shown in your second screenshot.
As such, I am not yet convinced that the shortened URL would not:
** Resolve in full in the browser, thereby exposing the name of our internal platform as well as personal data about the driver; and
** Lead to Bolt’s own error page rather than the shortener’s error page.
* In general, URL shorteners do not work in the way described in your message. By design, a shortener simply creates a redirect: when a user clicks the shortened link, the browser follows the redirect to the original destination. At that point, the full destination URL is displayed in the browser’s address bar. This is how all mainstream browsers handle redirects, and the shortener has no ability to prevent it.
In our case, that means the shortened link will always resolve to the full Admin URL once clicked. If the user does not have the right certificates, the system will show Bolt’s own error page, but the Admin link itself (including “admin” in the structure and the driver’s partner ID) will already be exposed.
The only way for a shortener to avoid showing the full destination URL would be if it acted as a proxy: fetching the destination itself and displaying a custom error page in its own interface. That would require the third-party shortener to actually access Bolt Admin links on its servers. This would still amount to disclosing Admin and personal data to the shortener provider, and is therefore even more problematic.
For these reasons, URL shorteners cannot prevent the underlying Admin link from being revealed. Masking with a shortener is not a security measure, and it does not change the fact that sharing Admin links externally exposes both internal system details and driver personal data.
* Overall, the key issue is not whether the content of Admin can be accessed, it is that the identifier and the internal system name are exposed externally in the first place. This counts as both a disclosure of personal data and an exposure of our internal systems, which is why, as a rule, Admin links cannot be shared outside Bolt.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
# Competitive context
{panel}

* We understand the strong business rationale behind this proposal and the need to stay competitive in the Georgian market. That said, we must remain careful in how such solutions are implemented. Even in a competitive environment, exposing Admin or driver identifiers externally is not acceptable, and would carry significant regulatory and reputational risks for Bolt. 
* Out of curiosity, do you know how competitors are approaching this type of feature from a technical and compliance perspective? It would be helpful for us to understand what practices are actually being used in the market.

I hope the above clarifies where our advice. I am happy to discuss if anything is unclear.

{quote}Thank you for coming back to us on this.

To clarify our intent regarding the annualised inflow guarantee: this point is included in the contract to provide stability for both sides. When the original pricing structure was agreed with Taavi, the basis was 20,000 units annually. Later discussions with Neeme referred to 40,000 units, which would have provided the necessary volume for us to keep pricing sustainable and plan resources effectively.

With the latest figure reduced to 10,000 units, the overall volumes no longer match the assumptions behind the pricing offer. The inflow guarantee therefore helps us ensure that, even if volumes fall short, there is a mechanism to cover part of the shortfall so that we can still maintain service capacity and quality.

Practically speaking, we would not bill for the full shortfall in units. Instead, we would apply the recovery rate achieved to date (for example, if there was a shortfall of 1,000 units and our YTD recovery rate was 50%, the guarantee would only be applied to 500 units). This keeps the arrangement fair and linked to actual outcomes.

+*THOUGHTS*+

* Push notification:
** Counts as direct comms, but not directly promotional (as research focused - in any event, not from third-party). As such, opt-in consent not required (as does not count as direct marketing), and overall low risk.
* Survey:
** Data collection here is low risk. Covered in ‘survey’ section of the driver privacy notice.
** Collection of survey data is based on legitimate interest. Use of contact information is based on consent, as we ask for it in the form - this is fine.
** Technically, collection of the data is based on legitimate interest here, rather than consent. However, it is helpful that we are asking for the driver’s preference on whether they want to be contacted - this minimises risk.
** We should only retain the survey results for as long as we need them,

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Advise that we can proceed (provided not promotional - _research_ survey), but retain results only for as long as is necessary (/)

*a.* Such a situation cannot occur. If a driver registers as a legal entity on the Bolt platform, this means that the respective legal entity enters into the Agreement with Bolt (T&Cs) upon submitting the registration form. In that case, a contract is formed between Bolt and the legal entity that engages the driver (whether as a contractor or employee), and all payments are made to that legal entity.

*b.* There is no contradiction. The legal entity becomes a party to the Agreement with Bolt, but only a natural person can physically perform the transportation service and is the recipient of the service provider’s card for taxi services. Section 2.4 therefore, clarifies that both the legal entity (as the contractual party) and the individual driver (as the service performer) are jointly and severally liable if there is a breach.

* After the Restructuring, *Bolt Local will be responsible* for all reclassification-related liabilities that accrue *after* *the transfer*. However, it can be argued that *Bolt Ops remains jointly liable with Bolt Local for a period of 5 years* for obligations under driver agreements that are transferred to Bolt Local — if the localization qualifies as a transfer of business under Estonian law (this risk cannot be eliminated and will be assessed by court in case of dispute). Practically speaking, the risk may be limited, as Dutch authorities or individual claimants are unlikely to be aware of this specific Estonian legal provision that applies in the event of a business transfer.

{color:#ff5630}+*Potential risks:*+{color}

* *Advertising and Misrepresentation Risks* - the wording _“Your chance to get £50”_ could be construed as a guaranteed reward. I note the follow-up text clarifies it’s conditional on being selected and completing an interview, but that isn’t stated upfront.
* *Employment / Worker Status Risk* - offering “incentives” could be interpreted as closer to an employment-style benefit if phrased as guaranteed compensation. Keeping it explicitly tied to optional research participation helps reduce this risk. We should avoid language that suggests taking part in the survey is part of working conditions or pay.
* *Incentives & Tax Implications* - offering a £50 digital gift card could be viewed as taxable income. While responsibility may rest with the participant, Bolt should clarify in T&Cs that participants are responsible for reporting any tax liability.
* *Fairness / Selection Criteria* - because some respondents will be “disqualified” (Q1 and Q2), it’s important to make this clear to avoid complaints from drivers who expected £50 but didn’t qualify.

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

Bolt’s global greenhouse gas emissions including emissions from the ride-hailing service are calculated annually. 

Based on vehicle make, model and and year, we determine the associated fuel type and from that the emission factor. 

The emission factor is multiplied by the order mileage i.e. the distance of each order.

* Measurement period : 11Aug2025 - 10Sep2025
* The branding had a positive effect on *FTRs* during the measurement period, generating *60 incremental activations daily* (59% of total arrival activations) with a *1Y GMV of €122.5*.
* We couldn't measure the impact on *All Rides* because we were unable to find a stable relationship between "to airport" and "from airport" rides prior to the branding period.
* The branding generated an average *incremental ROI* (incremental GMV/Cost) of *5.7* during the measurement period.

I checked the battery from Riga. Same kind of crack as on the brand new ones. The crack was not noticeably bigger than on the new caps.

Me and [~accountid:5e4a421e691b8a0c95c2cdec] tested the caps today using two different methods:

* Torquing the nuts to see at what point the nut fails. 
** Both sides (cracked and not cracked) withstood the 1.5Nm that we have specified in SOP (/) 
** Both sides (cracked and not cracked) started failing at around 2-2.5Nm, there was no noticeable difference between the cracked and not cracked side
** When the nut fails, it does not spin around or pull out completely. 
** The cracked side usually fails by opening up the crack and thus letting the nut move. The not cracked side breaks near the bottom end of the nut, which lets the nut slip.
* Pulling force for single nut using pallet jack and scale
** Despite the crack, both the nuts are fixed firmly in the plastic. When you start pulling out, the lower step of the nut holds it securely and it will not pull out easily.
** All the tested nuts could last 200kg pulling force. We saw a maximum of 300kg on the scale once, but as the scale is rated up to 200kg, we can not be certain in the precision. In one case the nut split in half, lower end still staying inside the cap.



*Conclusion*

The caps are stronger than initially thought and from the current test results I would be confident using them until we get replacements. However we must wait for the vibration test results before proceeding.

[~accountid:5b392195d394412e188f0957] I confirm the bug in PRELIVE. The bug doesn’t manifest for your user, but it works 100% for user {{alexandru.niculae}}

Execute {{node tooling_scripts/make-request.js --env prelive -s directory -e internal/getAllUsersOrganisationalInfo -m POST -f -d ‘' | grep alexandru.niculae}} and you’ll get empty result.
Try {{node tooling_scripts/make-request.js --env prelive -s directory -e internal/getAllUsersOrganisationalInfo -m POST -f -d ‘' | grep Alexandru.Niculae}} and the result is {{"Alexandru.Niculae@bolt.eu": {}} → you get the Pascal case 

If the {color:#ff5630}*login is extracted from the email address*{color}, it would be {{Alexandru.Niculae}} and you would expect this to work: {{node tooling_scripts/make-request.js --env prelive -s directory -e internal/getMultipleManagementChains -m POST -f -d '{"logins": ["Alexandru.Niculae"]}'}}, but it doesn’t, it returns empty result. However, providing it in lowercase {{node tooling_scripts/make-request.js --env prelive -s directory -e internal/getMultipleManagementChains -m POST -f -d '{"logins": ["alexandru.niculae"]}'}} produces the management chain.

----

We can consider this inconsistency (bug) at 2 levels of depth:

1. The low level / specific problem with endpoint {{internal/getMultipleManagementChains}} → It returns data from an in-memory cache that is populated with [emails transformed to lowercase|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/9d5c250254e1a2c6e619198a7e942f623a7dd9d1/src/foundation/data/directory_service/main/siem/SIEMRequester.ts#L177]. When login provided in the request is NOT lowercase, then it will never be found in the cache. The obvious / *simplistic fix* here would be to patch all methods in {{src/foundation/data/directory_service/main/service/Service.ts}} that take the {color:#ff5630}*okta login as input and make it lowercase*{color}. It would instantly remove the effect.

2. *The root cause of this mess is the organic development of those systems' integration* {color:#ff5630}*without clear definition for what each login is* {color}*(admin account, okta account, workday account etc) and what are their* {color:#ff5630}*business limits (character set, rules of composition)*{color}. If these were defined, then all parts of the systems should simply adhere to them and enforce them. What happens now is that we have some vague implicit rules set by whomever implemented parts of the system, but they are completely disconnected because nobody thought about the system in its entirety. For example: “login” means different things for different endpoints exposed by {{directory_service}}, it can be email address, admin panel user, github user, okta user… you would have to check the implementation to know what you’re supposed to provide. {color:#ff5630}*Although it looks superficially easy to fix the reported problem as suggested in point (1), the correct approach would be first to understand those terms, how are they used, disambiguate them, define some limits and align all system using them*{color}. The particular edge case / bug that you reported would be yet another piece of a much larger problem.

----

My concrete proposal is the following:

a) Implement point (1) to get rid of the effect

b) Reach out to SRE and understand why are not email addresses written in lowercase, which is the de facto rule in Bolt → I suspect someone writes them by hand in some system (Okta, Workday etc) and they are simply translated through Okta to {{directory_service}}. The goal is to patch ALL existing email addresses at the source and enforce input validation or sanitization at the source, so even if someone tries to write an email like {{Mihai.Casandra@BOlT.Eu}} it will always be recorded in the system as {{mihai.casandra@bolt.eu}}. I already reached out to [~accountid:712020:6051a399-1d8d-4067-8ca4-4776ebcad004] to check what can be done from Okta/Workday side. Will post an update when I find out more.

c) Independent of points (a) and (b), start a re-architecture effort to clean up those ambiguous endpoints and user concepts. I understand this is not high priority, but it ought to be done eventually. It will only get worse as we add more complexity to the admin-okta-workday integration.

Thank you for sharing the proposed terms with _A Nossa Farmácia_. After reviewing the request, we would like to highlight the following legal and operational considerations:

# *Legal Framework*

* Under Portuguese law, only pharmacies and MNSRM outlets that are duly registered with INFARMED may sell and deliver OTC medicines online or to customers’ homes. Being such a large group of pharmacies, we already know that _A Nossa Farmácia_ is properly licensed, but it is important to have this in mind and I think this should be verified anyway.
* The transport of medicines to the patient’s home is subject, with the necessary adaptations, to the transport rules set out in the Good Distribution Practices of medicines.
* Deliveries must be executed under the supervision of appropriately qualified personnel (pharmacists or pharmacy technicians), ensuring compliance with Good Distribution Practices (GDP) for packaging, temperature control, and security.
* Article 2(2) of _Portaria n.º 1427/2007_ requires that home delivery must be supervised by a pharmacist (for pharmacies) or a pharmacist/pharmacy technician (for OTC outlets). Article 3(3) further establishes that home delivery can only be assured by the pharmacy or the authorised point of sale where the medicine was requested.

On this basis, *our legal assessment first concluded that, strictly interpreted, delivery should be handled directly by the pharmacy or licensed outlet*—not by a third-party courier without such supervision.

That said, *we understand that there is room for interpretation: the requirement could also be understood as meaning that the pharmacist/technician must supervise the preparation, packaging, and sealing of the order* before handing it over to the courier, rather than being physically responsible for the delivery to the customer.

Both Uber and Glovo appear to operate under the interpretation that the pharmacist’s supervision at the preparation stage is sufficient.

However, it is important to note that in the [Q&A part of INFARMED website|https://www.infarmed.pt/web/infarmed/perguntas-frequentes-area-transversal/medicamentos_internet] we can read the following:

*_A farmácia pode enviar os medicamentos por correio ou estafeta?_*

_Não, a legislação determina que os medicamentos devem ser entregues ao domicílio respeitando as normas de supervisão, habilitação e formação adequada à dispensa de medicamentos e respeitar as regras de transporte previstas nas boas práticas de distribuição de medicamentos._
_As Boas Práticas de Distribuição de Medicamentos determinam:_
 _"(...) 9.4 - Os medicamentos devem ser transportados em todo o seu circuito por forma que:_
_a) Não se perca a sua identificação;_
_b) Não contaminem nem sejam contaminados por outros produtos ou materiais;_
_c) Sejam adoptadas precauções especiais contra o derrame, a rotura ou o roubo;_
_d) Estejam em condições de segurança e não sejam sujeitos a condições inapropriadas de calor, frio, luz, humidade ou outros factores adversos, nem à acção de microrganismos ou agentes infestantes._
_9.5 - Os medicamentos que necessitem de controlo da temperatura durante o armazenamento devem igualmente ser transportados em condições especiais adequadas.(...)"_.

EN: 
*_Can the pharmacy send medicines by post or courier?_*

_No. Legislation requires that medicines must be delivered to the home in compliance with the rules on supervision, qualification and adequate training for the dispensing of medicines, and in accordance with the transport rules set out in the Good Distribution Practices of Medicines._

The Good Distribution Practices of Medicines establish that:
_“(...) 9.4 – Medicines must be transported throughout their entire route in such a way that:_
_a) Their identification is not lost;_
_b) They do not contaminate nor are contaminated by other products or materials;_
_c) Special precautions are taken against spillage, breakage or theft;_
_d) They are kept in safe conditions and not subjected to inappropriate conditions of heat, cold, light, humidity or other adverse factors, nor to the action of microorganisms or pests._
_9.5 – Medicines requiring temperature control during storage must also be transported under appropriate special conditions. (...)”_

So, again, therefore, although this could be considered a grey area, INFARMED’s position appears to be clear, even if the response is supported by other considerations.

For this reason, we believe that, although the primary liability lies with the pharmacy, as they are the direct addressees of the applicable regulation, *Bolt can still be questioned* *by the authorities* *and might be subject to fines*, and +*we should remain mindful of this risk*+.

In case it is decided to move forward, besides the risks that were flagged:

# *Operational Considerations:*

* Bolt cannot guarantee that a courier will voluntarily return an undelivered order to the pharmacy. However, we can commit to directing the courier back to the pharmacy when delivery is not possible.
* Concerning the _not delivering simultaneously any other order from other partners_ we think there isn’t a major problem, as long as you are operationally able to do this. We just need to make it clear that we can only provide such assurance with respect to Bolt deliveries, but not regarding deliveries from other platforms that the courier may be carrying out.
* We should be prepared to compensate couriers in cases where they are required to return orders to the pharmacy.
* Customer Support (CS) teams must be fully briefed on this process so they can provide clear instructions to couriers who encounter delivery issues.
* As per article 3(2) of _Portaria n.º 1427/2007_ _,_ _“the dispensing of medicines with home delivery is limited to the municipality where the pharmacy is located and to the neighbouring municipalities”._



Having in consideration our assessment, please let us know how you want to proceed.

Thank you!

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

** You probably don’t need to provision extra; 125 MB/s → 25 GiB dump finishes in ~3–4 min.
* *Performance*: local, predictable, fastest restarts.
* *Ops overhead*: you have 400 volumes to track; but with Terraform/automation it’s manageable.
* *Scaling*: cost grows linearly with node count, whether or not dumps ever happen.

----

h3. *Option B — Shared FSx for Lustre (multi-AZ)*

* *FSx cost model*: depends on deployment type:
** *Persistent 1*: starts around $0.14/GB-month plus throughput capacity.
** *Persistent 2*: $0.025/GB-month, but lower per-TB throughput.
** *Scratch*: billed only for storage during use, suited for temporary jobs.
* *Throughput*:
** Much higher than EFS, HPC-grade (hundreds of MB/s).
** A 25 GiB dump at ~200–400 MB/s finishes in ~1–2 min.
* *Ops overhead*:
** One FSx per Region (with 3 AZ mount targets).
** Install Lustre client ({{amazon-efs-utils}} equivalent for FSx) on every node.
** Mount and manage one shared filesystem instead of 400 separate volumes.
* *Scaling*:
** Same fixed cost whether 5 dumps or 500.
** At low usage (5–10 dumps/month), the *base cost dominates*.
* *Risk*: network FS → if FSx hiccups, dumps stall; restarts delayed.

----

h1. 💰 Example monthly costs

_(ballpark, ignoring snapshot charges, all us-east-1)_

* *EBS option (400 × 25 GiB gp3)*:
25 GB × 400 × $0.08 ≈ *$800/month*
* *FSx Lustre Persistent 2 (1 TiB, multi-AZ)*:
1024 GB × $0.025 ≈ *$25/month* storage
** throughput capacity (say 50 MB/s baseline ~$2/TiB-month)
** multi-AZ surcharge
→ *$50–70/month total*
* *FSx Lustre Persistent 1 (1 TiB)*:
1024 GB × $0.14 ≈ *$140/month*
** throughput capacity (higher)
→ *$200+/month*

👉 So: FSx could be *an order of magnitude cheaper* than 400 idle EBS volumes if your dump frequency is really near-zero.

----

h1. ⚖️ Trade-off summary

*EBS per node*

* ✅ Predictable, fastest writes, zero network dependency
* ✅ Simple (no client modules, no shared FS)
* ❌ Scales cost linearly (≈ $800/mo for 400 nodes) even if no dumps ever occur

*FSx Lustre*

* ✅ Shared cost across fleet (tens to low hundreds $/mo)
* ✅ HPC-grade throughput for sequential writes
* ❌ Requires Lustre client on all nodes
* ❌ Network dependency → dumps may take longer than local EBS
* ❌ Higher ops complexity than “just attach EBS”

----

h1. 📝 Recommendation for our case (400+ nodes, rare dumps)

* If cost control is priority: *FSx Lustre Persistent 2* (multi-AZ) is attractive — you pay maybe $50–100/month fleet-wide instead of $800.
* If _fastest restart_ matters more than cost: *tiny per-node EBS* is still the safest, because dump writes don’t depend on network/storage service availability.
* Hybrid is possible:
** *EBS on a canary subset (say 20 nodes)* to guarantee some dumps with fastest restart.
** *FSx Lustre* as the fallback shared sink if more nodes crash.

+*Background*+

* Currently, drivers mark themselves when they have arrived.
** When they do so, ‘free waiting time’ starts. This can create problems where the driver pre-emptively marks themselves as having arrived, as waiting time is over before the driver gets there. Can lead to cases of driver fraud.
** Currently, if we identify that the driver is 300m away, we display a warning to the driver to confirm if their location is correct. 
* Proposed solution is to notify driver arrival through a detection process.
** Bolt’s geo team will use a set of mixed signals (ETA, GPS location, car speed etc) to send a signal to the rider to notify them when the driver has arrived. Free waiting timer then starts immediately and automatically.
*** NB. Drivers can still select when they have arrived. Auto-arrival only acts as an assist, not a restriction. If driver does not select arrived themselves, effectively a timer starts when the driver is there according to the signals, after which they are considered as ‘arrived’.
*** If driver selects arrived and is not close enough, the waiting time is paused.
** Auto-arrival switched off for airports due to high GPS inaccuracy.
* Seemingly launched last year in limited markets (including Portugal).
* A/B test will happen on 29 September (global - see rollout tracker).
** Only flagged on UK channel on 16 September.

+*Analysis*+

* Risk profile = Medium.
* Purpose / Legal basis:
** Purpose = To improve the transportation services in connecting passengers with drivers.
*** Legal basis = Contractual necessity (as necessary for costs / trip calculation). Fallback of legitimate interest if needed.
** Purpose = To prevent fraudulent activity.
*** Legal basis = Legitimate interest.
* Transparency:
** We can argue this is covered in the updated privacy notice. Thank goodness.
* DPIA:
** There is a risk of false positives here. Also invisible processing and live location tracking, in a way that may affect what a driver is paid and what a rider is charged.
** As such, a DPIA would be prudent.
* ADM:
** System is automated (although this is mitigated by driver’s ability to manually mark arrival, which preserves driver control and ensures this is an assist rather than a restriction).
** We can argue is does not produce a significant effect - It helps, and is an assist rather than a restriction.
** Ideally we would have disclaimer language / an appeals process here, but there is unlikely to be operational appetite for this.
* Fairness / accuracy:
** If errors in the system, this could result in unfair charges / cancellations (particularly with airports). We need to ensure it is accurate.

+*Next Steps*+

* Questions:
** Are we just looking at ETA, GPS location and car speed here? What else?
** What happens if a driver believes this has been incorrectly applied? Can they challenge?
* Advice to business:
** We can proceed with the initiative.
** This is subject to the following:
*** We are only collecting the data that is strictly necessary to do this.
*** Decision-making process here should be clearly documented (i.e., datapoints and how it works), in case we are ever challenged on this.
*** Logic should be applied to minimise the risk of false positives and ensure clear lines of accountability if anything goes wrong.
*** Since the UX has already been developed, it would be good to have a driver article on this so that they understand how this works.
*** Have some sort of ability for users to challenge this if it results in unfairness.
* Privacy actions (NB. Completely swiftly and pragmatically, as Privacy Team looped in late).

Hi Costică,

 

Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *1 September 2025.*Please see our response below.

 

*Location tracking* 

 

It’s important to emphasize the difference between “Allow all the time” and “Allow while using the app” location tracking settings from a technical perspective:

 

* “Allow all the time” access means the application can track a Driver’s phone’s location as follows:
** The Driver is *offline* (i.e., has explicitly set their status as offline to not provide the services): the location of the Driver is tracked only when the application screen is open.
** The Driver is *online* (i.e., the Driver explicitly chose to set their status as online to provide the services): the location of the Driver is tracked when the application screen is open or the application is running in the background.
** In both scenarios, the Driver’s location is not tracked when the application is fully closed.
** For clarity, an application is considered to be “running in the background” when a Driver opens another application or returns to their phone’s home screen without closing the original application. In this state, the original application remains active and can perform tasks even though it is not currently visible on their screen.
* “While using the app” access means the application only tracks the Driver’s phone’s location when the application’s screen is open and the Driver is actively interacting with it. Once the Driver puts the application in the background, it stops receiving location updates. This access means the application can only access a Driver’s phone’s location when it’s visible on their screen. If the Driver switches to another application or the phone’s screen turns off, the application won’t receive location updates in the background.

 

To provide transportation services via Bolt Platform, Drivers are required to grant Bolt the permission to access their location data in "_Allow all the time_" mode. It is important to note that Bolt does not continuously track or access Driver location data 24/7 when "_Allow all the time_" permission is granted. This setting is essential to ensure the Bolt Driver Application functions properly when Drivers go online. It allows access to the Driver's location data both when the application screen is open and running in the background, enabling critical features such as accurate Passenger-Driver matching and real-time route optimization. These functions ensure that the Bolt Driver Application operates as intended and without interruptions, enabling seamless service provision to Passengers. 

 

*Purpose Limitation*

 

As outlined above, Drivers who want to provide transportation services via the Bolt Driver Application have to enable the "Allow all the time" location setting. This permission is essential to ensure the proper functioning of the critical features of the Bolt Driver Application.

As mentioned above, granting "Allow all the time" access by Drivers does not mean that Bolt continuously tracks or accesses location data at all times, in particular when the Driver is offline or the Bolt Driver Application is fully closed.

* On iOS, "Allow all the time" access permission is required by Bolt only when Drivers go online using the Bolt Driver Application. This permission ensures that the Driver's location data is collected whenever the Bolt Driver Application is open and running in the background while the Driver is online and providing services.
* The "Allow all the time" location permission is required for Android devices due to new policies and technical specifications introduced in Android 14. This update requires Bolt to ask Drivers to select the “Allow all the time” access permission to ensure that location data is collected whenever the Bolt Driver Application is open and running in the background while the Driver is online and providing services. This change was introduced through a software update to the Bolt Driver Application to align with these updated policies and ensure uninterrupted operation of the Bolt Driver Application. Despite this adjustment in how permissions are labeled, communicated to Drivers or managed on Android devices, the fundamental location tracking logic remains unchanged. Bolt continues to track Driver location only when they go online and the Bolt Driver Application is open or running in the background.

Whether on iOS or Android, location tracking occurs only when the Bolt Driver Application screen is open or the Driver is online with the Bolt Driver Application running in the background, enabling Bolt to maintain high levels of efficiency and service quality that Drivers and Passengers rely on.

Hi [~accountid:712020:b3dbddb5-16a8-4ad6-9138-80fbe6e695a9], my research on this suggests that under Article L. 3122-4 of the Code des Transports, PHV drivers are required to have:

* Vehicle insurance explicitly covering paid passenger transport (_assurance à titre onéreux_),
* Professional liability insurance (_Responsabilité Civile Professionnelle_, or *RC Pro*), and
* Registration in the VTC national register (plus associated vehicle and driver documentation).

The _key point of divergence_ from taxis is that the RC Pro is listed as a separate, additional requirement for VTCs and not bundled into vehicle insurance by default. This differs from taxis, where the “taxi package” insurance often covers both in practice and in law. 

So in my understanding, the “taxi package” is common practice for taxis; however, it is not necessarily automatic for PHVs. In light of this, we coudl respond that this logic _could_ apply to PHVs, the compliance check would need to be stricter as to ensure that : 

* The RC Pro is either provided separately, *or*
* Is unambiguously covered within the _assurance à titre onéreux_ certificate submitted.


What do you think? 

Thank you in advance for your feedback ! 🙏

Hi[~accountid:712020:8623c4b8-46b3-4c5d-b18a-e6e3f080ca20], 

When a company enters judicial liquidation in France, all payments must be handled exclusively through the appointed court liquidator. The former company director is no longer entitled to receive payments directly, and doing so would be contrary to the legal process. Any payment made outside of the liquidation procedure—especially to a personal bank account—would be irregular and may expose us to liability or future recovery claims.

h3. Next Steps

# *Request Information on the Liquidation Procedure:*

* Has the company provided any documentation from the liquidator (e.g., judgment of liquidation, contact details of the mandataire judiciaire)?
* Can they provide the _judicial liquidation reference number_ and the court decision?

# *Do Not Proceed with Payment:*

* Any payments should only be made to a bank account controlled by the *court-appointed liquidator*.

For cases where refund was issued but can’t be seen on the user’s card or Bolt balance.

* Check where the refund was sent to and if it was successful on the [transaction history page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%2265766018%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] 
** If Bolt balance refund is successful, there is a green button after the refund “🟢 success”
** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds
* Check if the user did not have a previous debt or previous failed payment that was covered up with the refund
* If refund was sent to Balance instead of card, check first if payment was made from card. Usually, if card payment fails, card refund also fails. Sometimes refund will be sent to balance in cases payment was charged from balance first as debt and the refund will clear the debt previously created by the balance charge. 
* Check [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/1946767063], to ensure there are no errors on the refund and advise the user to check with their bank if card refund was successfully completed.
** If there is an error, escalate to Commerce > Ride Hailing/Food/Rentals payments
* Only successful card payments can be refunded to card.
